text.p: Lichfield
Janry ye 21 1733
Hond Sir.

It is not to be expressed ye Joy that the family was in at ye Receipt of Dear Poppa's Letter, which we Received the 7th of this Month. My Poor Momma was in very good Spirits two or three Days after she received your Letter, but now begins to grow maloncolly again, and has little ugly fainting fits, she is in great hopes of ye Transports going for you every Day, for we Please our selves with ye hopes of your spending this Summer with ye Family. My Momma rec'd ye thirty Pounds you was so good to send her, she has Paid ten Pounds to Mr Rider for one Year's Rent, and ten Pounds to the Baker, and if you can spare a little more as you tell her you will, she is in hopes of paying all ye Debts, that you may have nothing to fret you when you come home. My Momma staid six Weeks in London after you left her at Mr Bronker's, for she was very much out of order when she was there, and they would not part with Her before & was very good to her. Mr Adair came twice to see my Momma at Mr. Bronker's, & was prodigiously civil and obliging, and begged her to send him some Ale, which she designs to do very soon: My Momma paid for your Stockings & Holland as soon as you left her, and as soon as She came down to us, not to her great Joy, she found us very shabby in Clothes, & in all our accoutrements, that we was rather like so many beggars than Gentlemen Soldiers, but with much ado at last she equipped us out a little better, & now with a great Deal of Mending & Patching we are in Statue quo . We received a Letter from Brother Peter, which was directed to you, and we thought it would be too troublesome to send it enclosed, so have sent you a Copy of it on ye other side. at Present we have but little News, Doctor Hector is married to Miss Pop Smith, & Mr Lawrence who is at London is married to ye Lady who you saw at Captn Goddard's a very pretty Woman (only she squints a little, (as
Captn Brazen says in ye Recruiting officer) Captn Weldon has parted with his Commission, and has half Pay as Lieutenant of a Man of War, every Body loves & likes Mrs Weldon, but he has quarrelled with most of ye People in this Place, which gives ye poor Woman a great deal of uneasiness, but they are both highly Civil to our family. Mr & Mrs Harvey came to see my Momma as soon as she came to Town, she is a very fine Lady & has returned but few of her visits, I am a great favourite of both of them and am with them every Day. Mr Walmisley has had a very great quarrel with Captn Malcolm & I think (Considering he being always so civil to ye Officers) used him very ill, but at Present all is over, but they don't visit one another. I have been to Mr Ofleys who sent a Man & horse for me with Mr & Mrs Harvey & Mr Walmisley, were I got acquainted with his two Sons, who are fine young Gentlemen, Mr Walmisley gave me slyly, half a crown for ye Butler & another for ye Groom, for my self, which made me look very grand. All ire friends are very well, we had a letter from My Uncle Day, who says that Mr Lowe preached a Sermon which was thought by every body one of ye Best they had heard for a long Time. Mrs Lowndes sends love & Service, but has not yet conquered her fever, My Grandmother is very poorly & sends her blessing, & would fain live to see you once more, my Brothers & Sisters their Duty and am in a particular manner
Dear Sr Ire ever Dutiful Son
David Garrick
P.S. Dr Sir if you could possibly send Mr Walmisley a little Wine, I am sure he would take it as a Particular Favour
Lichfield June ye 16th 1733
Hond Sir

We received ire two last Letters one that came by ye Surgeon's Mate and the other which came by Your Lieutenant. It is the greatest Pleasure We have in your absence to hear of Ire being in a good state of health. I write to you the Beginning of May last in which Letter I gave you an account of my Sister Jenney's Illness, but I suppose you have not received, by ire not mentioning any thing of it in Ire Letters, but I hope you received it soon after ire Last came away. She has been most half a Year confined to the house, but she is now upon the mending hand, Doctor Hector has taken a great deal of Care of her, and Mr Morgan got ye advice of a very top Physician at London, whose Perscriptions he sent down which she has taken, and we find she is much recovered by them, but she is not as yet fit to stir abroad. My Poor Momma with attending My Sister Jenny got a Fever upon her Spirits which forced her to keep her Room for a fortnight, but she is pretty well recovered. My Momma designs to try her interest to get you leave to come over by next spring if you are not sent for over before. she designs to apply first to the Brigadier. My Momma will get Mr Harvey to write her a pretty Letter to ye Brigadier ye Purport of it shall be this, that you having a Son to put out, and My Momma being incapable to do it herself, it would be a great detriment to the Family if you was not hear to do it your self, and as soon as Mr Harvey has done it, My Momma will copy it, and send it to Mr Adair to give it to ye Brigadier. Mr
Walmisley is gone to Scarborough with My Lord and Lady Huntington. Mr Perkins is cited into ye Court for Drunkenness & swearing by Mr Rider. Mr Sharpless has lost a Tankard of twelve Pounds which was stole from him, and there is a Dragoon in Goal upon Suspicion. The Dragoons are Removed to Burton throe ye Interest of Mr Plummer, but Mr Harvey and his Lady remains at Lichfield, she has lately lain in, and ye Child has been Baptised and My Momma was invited to it. He Has lately come from London and has brought me two Pair of large Silver Buckles one Pr for my Shoes & ye other for my Breeches knees, and Mr Walmisley a fine Snuff Box. He wishes every Day to see you at Lichfield and always drinks in a Bumper our friends at Gibraltar. there is great talk that his Brother My Lord Harvey will be made Secretary of War. I think Dear Sr I have wrote you all ye News I can think of. Mrs Lowndes sends her love & service to her Master, My Grandmother her Blessing and all she desires to live to see you again. My Brothers and Sisters their Duty and I, who am with the greatest Sincerity Dear Sir
Ire most Dutiful Son
David Garrick
PS We have not heard from my Brother Peter Since I sent you the Copy of ye Letter -
To Captn Garrick in Brigadier Kirks Regiment at Gibraltar.
Lichfield
September ye 12th 1733
Dear Sir.

We received yours dated ye 19th of July, and We All have been very uneasy to hear you have not been well, and hope that at the receiving of this you'll have got ire Stomach up again. All the Family is pretty well except my Grandmother who is often out of order, and so indeed is Mrs Lowndes: and Jenny is perfectly recovered. My Momma has spoke to Mr Walmisley and to Mr Rider, the first has spoke to Mr Plummer, who has promised to use his interest, to get You leave to come for England to vote for him, and Mr Walmisley has set you in ye list among the Voters, and has made over a Burgess to you to qualify you for voting, without taking any Oath, So we are in great hopes we shall see You in ye Spring, or else my Momma is determined to come to you. Mr Christopher Lowe has been at Lichfield and has brought News of Peter, he says Mrs Jasper has had a Letter from Sr Chalener Ogle who tells him that he is vastly fond of him, and that he admires him for his Sobriety, Modesty, and good Humour, so we hope in a Little time to hear of his being made a Lieutenant. He is still aboard with the Admiral. This Letter Mr Lowe puts into the Secretary's Bag, and we shall be glad to know whether it comes soon to you, because of sending the
rest the same way. My Momma has write twice to Cousin Cazulett, and I believe she is very well satisfied. It was Sherbet, Lemon, Water, and Sugar, that Mrs Cazulett gave My Momma at Chelsea for a Looseness. Sr You was pleased to write in one of Your Letters when I should be fit for the University, I fancy in about two Years, I should have been ready by now, only my going to Lisbon beckoned me a great deal, but every body thinks at 18 or 19 Years of Age is time enough. All Your Children Join with me in Love and Duty, My Grandmother sends her Blessing, Mrs Lowndes her Love and Service together with Aunt Kinaston, and Cousin Bailye's family. Mrs one Night got tipsy by Dringing here is to all our Friends by Land and by Sea. Mr Walmisley sends his Service to Brigadier Colombine and Self. My Momma desires you'll send if possible to Mr Bronker some wine if announced to nobody else. My Momma sends her most tender affections and I am Dear Sr
Ire Most dutiful Son
David Garrick
To Captn Garrick in Brigadier Kirk's Regiment at Gibraltar.
Lichfield
Decembr ye 3d 1733
Dear Sr

We received Yrs Yesterday dated the last of Octobr which was great joy to all ire Family to hear you had so good health. My Momma spoke again Yesterday to Mr Walmisley, about Ire coming for England and he has promised her faithfully that he wont neglect it, for he goes to London Xmas. My Momma inquired about the Man Jasper Woodhouse, and his Friends were glad to hear he was alive, but wished they had known sooner, because they believed he had take possession of the Estate, and had spent a great deal of it, for he is a good for nothing fellow, this Woodhouse told Kent the Butcher and his wife how that his Brother Jasper died at his house in London and how that he took care of him when he was sick. the Estate is worth good £30 a Year, and that he is Heir to another of six score pound a Year My Momma has sent you enclosed an advertisement concerning this Woodhouse, which Web ye Baker sent us. We have great talk of War, but don't hear of any New Regiments to be raised, they say they are pressing Soldiers every day, Ten Men of War of 2d, 3d, & 4th rates are ordered into ye Mediterranean. Grand preparations are making for Prince of Oranges Wedding, which they say will be the 10th of this Month, it should have been sooner, but that he was taken ill at the Dutch chapel, he is mightily Liked by the Ladies, and indeed is generally by all. Mr Walmisley sends his service to you and to Brigadier Columbine. All our family is pretty well at present, except Mrs Lowndes who sends her love and service to you, and my grandmother her Blessing, and a great many thanks for what you mentioned of her in Ire last, all Ire Children send their Duty, and I am with the greatest Duty and affection
Yrs David Garrick
Lichfield
March ye 18th 1734

We had ye pleasure of receiving two of Ire Letters the one dated the 29th of Janry the other the 2d of Febry. I cant but tell my Dear Pappa that one part of his Letter put a damp upon my pleasure, in which you thought I was neglectful of Writing. It would be the worst of ingratitude, and I ought to be esteemed ye worst of Wretches, did I neglect, what I thought would give ye least pleasure and Satisfaction to one of the best of Fathers. If those Persons who have not in any measure received what tenderness & Affection, I have, from their Parents, are accounted Reprobates, if they omit to pay all ye Regard and obedience to them they possible can, what on ye contrary can be said for him who in every instance of Life, has had ye greatest indulgences from a most kind father, whose study has always been to promote the welfare of his Children, such a one I think that does not return Paternal love with filial affection is ye most odious Monster, and rather fit for ye Society of Brutes than that of Men; In my poor opinion Nature seems to have done her endeavour to have planted in him all ye contraries, to obedience, virtue, morality, gratitude and what is most commendable in any Young Person, tho He had but ye least share; of what Fartherly love & goodness, I enjoy. You have Dear Sir bestowed upon me a good Education, and I hope you'll find that as my understanding ripens, and as Learning, Virtue, and good qualifications are inculcated in me, I shall the better know ye Worth & value of so good a father. When I do but consider of what you find fault with me in ire Letter, I fancy to my self the most odious Ideas of a disobedient Son, and
rather than I will be upbraided with that worst of Names, I will employ for ye future my whole care & time to be found in every respect
Ire most obedient Son
David Garrick

I have spoke to Mr Walmisley who is not as yet gone to London, but as wrote to Mr Plummer, who says it is impossible to obtain leave, till it's certain whether there will be peace or War, but Mr Walmisley promises to do you all the Service that lies in his power, and if all this Noise and bustle should turn to a Peace (which is believed will be so) he does not doubt but of getting You leave to be absent from ye Regiment. We have not heard from Brother Peter since Mr Morgan had an account that he had received all his things that he sent him, & in that he hoped that he should not be any more expensive to You. My Momma sends her dearest Love & affection to You, and desires me to tell You that she has almost cleared all the Debts, except a little to ye Butcher, which she hopes to clear in a Month or two. We have had great rejoicings all over England, on account of the Nuptials of ye Prince of Orange with ye Princess Royal, every Body almost wears Orange Cockades & favours, houses are illuminated, Burnfires, Drinking ye healths of ye Royal couple, together with all ye Royal Family. Mr Walmisley treated the Ladies & Gentm at ye Assembly with Rack Punch, and presented ye Gentm with Cockades & ye Ladies with Favours, His House was illuminated from top to bottom, all ye Town came up to see it. most of ye Gentm of ye Town met at ye Swan, which was likewise illuminated. all sides and parties are extremely fond of the Prince of Orange, who is a very good Scholar, has a very fine address, complaisance to every body, has been entertained all over ye Kingdom, at the best towns, made several fine speeches, both Latin as well as English. Mrs Lowe & her Daughter are leaving Lichfield to go to their Son at London, who has taken ym a house at Brooke Green. My Grandmother has been very bad but now is pretty well recovered & hopes yet to see you before she dies; poor Mrs Lowndes too is almost constantly rolling about ye flower with ye Cholick or has her Head tide about with a Napkin with ye head Ach, like one that is a Victim for a Sacrifice, but I hope in a little time we shall cure her, for she rather mends of it.
Septbr ye 2nd 1734
Dear Sir.

We received Yrs dated ye 27th July, by which we find you have not as yet received one that My Lady Bidulph enclosed to her Brother wherein I gave you an account of our Soliciting for ye King's Leave for ire coming to England, We are still unresolved about that affair, but are in great hopes every Post of the good News. The reason that I have so long omitted writing, is, that our expectations for the King's permission being retarded by ye Rumours of a War, I waited and put the letter off till we were informed one way or the other, and are now expecting every Day News from London. Mr Plummer has made very great Interest and application above in ire Favour, through the instigation of Mr Walmisley who has taken true Pains to see it accomplis'd. Mr Plummer spoke twice to the Brigadier who at last promised not to oppose any application Mr Plummer shoul'd make above. My Momma spoke to Mr Moor about the Bill of Jasper Woodhouse, he told her he never had any thing to do with them, that his GrandMother was buried by the Parish, & his Mother was married again & lived at Birmingham, & if there was any thing she had it, his Parents were very Good sort of People & were well beloved & for that reason took great Care of his Grandmother. I have been very much desired by the Thrapps of this Town to enquire whether you had at Gibraltar one Simon Thrapp or if there was any Such Person, for they don't know whether he's dead or alive. My Momma has been extremely ill but still keeps her Room, tho we are in great hopes She is on the mending hand; Dr Hector has attended her for this fortnight who thinks She is quite
out of Danger Now, she has been afflicted with a great pain in her Side & vomittings. there is very little News stirring at Lichfield, they talk of War and very little else. My Momma sends her dearest loves to you & hopes to live to see you, My Grandmother sends her Blessing Mrs Lowndes love, We ire Children Our Duty who all are in great hopes of seeing You, which is the greatest Desire of
Sr Ire ever Dutiful Son
David Garrick
To Captn Garrick in Brigadier Kirk's Regiment at Gibraltar.
Lichfield
Decbr ye 23d 1734
Dear Sir.

We received a Letter from Mr Goddard and was vastly surprised to hear You had not received any Letter from us in four Months, having I'm sure wrote four which you don't make the least Mention of, and as I told Captn Goddard that if the Ships were as certain Carriers, as we were Writers, You would not I believe have any occasion to blame ire Son's Neglect. In three of my last Letters I gave You an account of my Mama's Illness which confined her to her Room for four Months, in which time she had several severe Relapses, and was exceedingly bad that Morning she received Mr Goddard's Letter which came very unseasonable, and was I'm sure no forwarder of her Recovery. We were forced to call in Doctor James who has been very diligent & careful to recover her, so beg if you can procure any of the peruvian Bark he mentions in his Letter, you will let him have it. My Mama's Disorder is a violent pain in her Hip & Thigh attended with a Fever on her Spirits, that
Nothing gives her ease but opium, and she has been easy these three Weeks. We were in Hopes of seeing You this Xmas, and expect every Post News from London; My Mama says she believes your presence would do more good than all the Physicians in Europe. Mr Morgan plagues Mr Arnold every Day who Promises very fair to do it this Day, and that Day so you may guess what expectations we live in, which if disappointed may cause a General indisposition throughout the Family. I wrote you word in one of my letters that Mr Bronkour was gone of for two thousand Pounds, & they say she'll sell coffee & Tea, &c, this Misfortune has cause grief to her Relations & Friends, Mr & Mrs Goddard are exceeding kind to them. Doctor James has so crested the Paper that I write upon it with the greatest Difficulty, so you must excuse Dear Sr the illshap'd Letters & crooked lines & impute them & other Faults to ye Doctor.
I am Sr Ire most Dutiful Son
David Garrick

P.S. I gave you an account in one of my letters (which I hope is received before this time) that my Mama had received No Money from Moor the Chandler with all the particulars. The Family & Friends send their usual loves, Duties, Services &c wishing you a Merry Xmas & happy New Year, and I think we have about three Xmas boxes owing us, if not four.
To Captn Garrick in Brigadier Kirk's Regiment at Gibraltar.

TEI.text:
Lichfield
Febry ye 17th 1735
Hond Sir.
With the usual Pleasure and Satisfaction We received ire Letter dated ye 17th of November with one enclosed for Willm Thrapp which I delivred to him with his Brother's Request for a small Matter to get clear with his Officer, They at first said they would consider of it, but after two or three Days cooling upon it, they desired I would send a Letter to him, but not a word of the Money, so I have omitted sending ye Letter till a better opportunity offers, for there is nothing in it that is of any consequence. My Momma was got very well and stirred abroad, but on the 9th of this Month she had a very severe Relapse which continued for a Week, but she is at present much better but very weak, attended with a Lowness of Spirits, which compels her to drink Wine which gives a great deal of uneasiness upon two accounts, as it goes against her inclination, and Pocket. We are making all possible interest we can for ire Leave to come over, we have not as yet had ye good News but Live in Daily expectation of it: Mr Walmisley is going to London very soon and he does not doubt but put the finishing stroke to it. We have a great many Officers here a Recruiting from Ireland, I was in great hopes I should have Recruited my Self this Spring, For Mr Harvey who is a Cornet in my Lord Car's Regnt had given me & Mr Walmisley a promise for his Commission, If his Brother in Law Sr Those Aston had died who at ye Time was struck with a dead Palsy, Mr Harvey being Heir to it through his Wife Sr Those Aston's Sister, or rather she was the Heiress; but Sr Thomas is now perfectly recovered. My Sister Lenney & Sister Jenny send their Duty to you and being in great Want for some Lace for Heads, and my Momma being but very Low in ye Purse by reason of her Illness could not afford ym so much Money, They with ye greatest Duty & Obedience request a small Matter to purchase their Head ornaments, great Necessity compels them to give you this Trouble, for they have never wore any thing else but plain head Clothes which hardly distinguishes them from ye Vulgar Madams. I have sent you Dear Sir the following Piece of Wit, hoping it may prove some Diversion to you Gibralterians, it was Delivered by ye Hands of a Halequin
at a late Masquerade, to all the People he Met, and delivred one also to the King upon his Knees, it was as follows.
G: R. by permission
This is to give Notice to all Gentlemen, Ladies, & Others, that at ye Opera House, in ye Hay Markett, this present Evening Will be presented ye Comical & Diverting Humours of Punch.
And on Thursday next, by ye Norfolk Company of Artificial Comedians, at Robin's great Theatrical Booth in Palace Yard, will be presented a Comical & Diverting Play of Seven Acts, called Court & Country, in which will be revived the entertaining Scene of ye two Blundering Brothers, with the Cheats of Rabbi Robin, Prime Minister to King Solomon: the whole concluding with a great Masque called the Downfall of Sejanus, or the Statesman's Overthrow: With Axes, Gibbets, & other Decorations proper to ye Play, to begin exactly at twelve o'clock.
N.B. There are a New set of Puppets as big as life, chief Part of which have been brought from ye Country, at a very great Expense. Vivant Rex et Regina.
Dear Sr If this impudent thing affords any Pleasure I have my Aim. All ye Family send their usual Blessing, Duty & Love.
I am Ire most Dutiful Son
David Garrick
To Captn Garrick in Brigadier Kirk's Regiment at Gibraltar.

text.p: Lichfield
April ye 24th 1735
Dear Sir.

As I have Ire Commands to write once a fortnight at least, nothing shall break my resolution of Giving Dr Papa as much Pleasure as lies in my little Power. You perhaps may think it Vain in me to call my Letters a sort of Pleasure, but as you was pleased to make me first vain by calling ym so, I shall easily get clear of ye imputation of Vanity: But then I know you'll readily make this objection, that you might call ym a Pleasure which would not at all be proper for me to do, as being my own; to this I answer, that I shall always esteem it a Virtue in Me, to follow my Father's steps at all times, & upon all occasions; tho I must & will confess, mine will be but a faint imitation of ye Original; But I may be like our Modern Painters who think they come near, nay some have ye Vanity to think they excel the ancient ones, but when they are compared there is as much difference between ym as there is between a Modern professed Painter, & a Sign Post dauber. Tho I must say There is one Piece of Le Grout's I value above all the Pieces of Zeuxis or Apelles, and I'll affirm, it gives me more Pleasure to have one glance of yt than to look a whole Day at the finest Pictures in ye World, nay it has this effect upon me, that whenever I look upon it I fancy my self at Gibraltar, I think I see the Spaniards, & sometimes I mount Garrison, and above all I very often by looking upon it think I see you, the Piece is in my hands, & I value it at a very great Price, I cant quite describe it to You, it is ye Figure of a Gentleman and I suppose military by his Dress, I think Le Grout told me his name was one Captn Peter Garrick, perhaps as you are in ye Army you
may know him, he is pretty Jolly & I believe Not very tall, I don't know what would be ye Consequence if he was at Lichfield, For my Poor Mama sighs whenever she passes ye Picture, you would be in Danger, I can tell you of Horns . My Friend Mr. Harvey is gone to quarters. I have received a most Friendly Letter from him. I can tell my Papa I stand a good chance to get into ye Army, I have the promise of three Lieutenant Colonels to provide for me. If they should get Regts one is Col. Warburton, Col. Fowkes, & Col. Pyot who has swore to make Chaplain to his Regt if I should be in orders. We have little or no News, so for want of News I'll send you a little Copy of Verses, I'll tell you ye Occasion Mr. Newton wrote a Copy of Verses to Miss Folly when he abuses ye Soldiers, Squires, & Beaux, so I was set on to answer ym having a little smattering yt way; I must write some of his Lines for the better understanding mine, he supposes himself in Love with her, & sends his Muse to tell her so, Mr Newton's Copy of verses is very long. I'll only send you the heads, yt I answered. Mr Newton calls it ye Discovery to Miss Folly his lines are as follow.
Go Muse and to ye Fair impart
The image of my lovesick Heart

(After follows a great many Fulsome Compliments to ye Lady which are too long to write here, and then he begins to complimt himself, in 8 lines which are full of Vanity, the lines are these, he speaks of his Lady.)

By ye Lover of the Muses, he means himself which is one of ye vainest things I ever read, I don't doubt but he loves ye Muses but I doubt very much whether he is beloved by ym; as he meddled with ye Soldiers I had good reason to take up ye Cudgels, mine are as follow.

I have not been very well, so you must forgive bad writing, spelling & blots. If you please to give ire self ye trouble of writing ye Verses over, you'll understand ym better. My Mama is very much mended if she holds it, she & all ye Family send their usual Love, Duty, blessing, & Service.
I am Dr Sr Ire ever Dutiful Son
David Garrick
To Captn Garrick in Brigadier Kirk's Regimt at Gibraltar.
Lichfield
May 1735
Dear Sr

Mr Pargiter being to set out to Morrow Morning for London, I would not omit the Opportunity of Letting my dear Father know a piece of News not only as it brings ye greatest joy to all ire Family, but also to Ire Self. Mr Rider who is made Chancellor has been up to Town & has got Brigadier Kirk's Leave & Interest for ire coming over to England; but you must not mention it to any Body till ire Orders come which will be very Soon. My Aunt Parkinson has sent for my Grand Mother & Sister Jenny to Chelsea who are there Now, & we hope will be there till ire Arrival in England. You will perhaps think me too Short as to Mr Rider being made Chancellor but the Affair is this, Mr Reins who was Chancellor for Lichfield is Dead, & the Bishop has put Mr Rider with his Eldest son into ye Patent. All Mr Riders friends, had ye Greatest Pleasure when they heard ye News, but We in a greater Degree from all ye Rest, We had ye Joyful News of his Success, & likewise his Success in getting My Dear Papa leave to come to England. My Mama is very poorly yet, All ye Family sends their usual Duty Love & Service and I am
Dr Sr Ire most obedt Son
David Garrick
Mr Pargiter waits for ye Letter so I must beg of you to pardon it's brevity.
My Sisters have received the Bill for the lace, & their Thanks are so abundant I have not Room to insert them. To Captn Garrick in Brigadier General Kirk's Regt at Gibraltar.
July 5th 1740
Dear Peter

I received Yrs with a double pleasure, Ire Safe Arrival & My Mother's better health being mentioned therein. I shall send the Sugar as p order & would have sent ye White wine but I thought the Grocers packing would be better & have put It of to a better Opportunity. I wrote to You by Mr Robin's & Sent Ire Wig; I hope before this You will have complied with ye Contents of It with regard to Giffard; My Lt Chamberlain has given him a very hopeful Answer, & I don't doubt of his Success. he has had Several friends back his Interest & I believe if You could any Ways Get a Lettr from Mr Webster whom You mentioned in Ire Last & is a very good Natured Man to One Mr Maddox to Use his Interest with ye Duke It would forward ye thing very much, if You tell how Giffard has recommended us, & that there is no great Obligation in such a trifle being only to Corroborate ye Interest he has already made, I am sure (& so is Brouncker who put this into Giffard's head) It would do him Service. I have ye Custom of ye Bedford Coffee house, one of ye best in London by Giffard's means; I would help him all
in our power, as I dare answer you would. Pray my best services to Mr Sudal & tell him his Nephew is at present very well tho he has been troubled with his old Disorder, I have got Drapar to take him to Dr Pellet a very Eminent Physician who has prescribed for him & I don't doubt but will relieve him; he is a very honest, sober sensible Young fellow & I don't doubt but will turn out well, he cannot get into ye Hospital till Michelmas, he is therefore advised till then to Attend Dr Nichols Lectures which will be of infinite Service to him & Serve by way of preparation to ye hospital Studies, I will take care of him till then & preach up Economy & Virtue to him; I have already given him a just detestation for ye lewd Night Walkers & vile polluters of Youth; he always smiles when I begin my Lecture & cries flee Ye, You talk welly as well as Mr Hinton, (a favourite Clergyman of his at Lichfield) Drapar gives him all ye Instruction he can & sends him to visit his patients every Day; he likewise tells me he is an understanding Youth & wants Nothing but a little polishing of his Dialect which has much of ye Staffordshire twang with It. I would advise Mr Sudal to Let him attend Dr Nicols Lectures, tell him I say so, & that Damn him I have a small veneration for his rotund Paunch & no despicable opinion of his Brains & that Likewise I have a much greater for the Rest of his family - I shall receive Mr. Kinaston's pension next Week & will give You Notice accordingly. I am glad My Mother is much better & I hope Each of Ire following Letters will Still give me more pleasure by the Same Account pray My Love & Service to Brothrs & Sisters & let know I will answer her letter when I can have Time to write a correct One.
I am Dr Peter Yrs Sincerely
D: Garrick
To Mr Peter Garrick at Lichfield, Staffordshire.
Dear Peter

I rec'd My Shirt safe & am now to tell You what I suppose You may have heard of before this, but before I let you into ye Affair tic proper to premise Some things that I may appear less culpable in ire Opinion than I might Otherwise do. I have made an Exact Estimate of my Stock of wine & What Money I have out at Interest & find that Since I have been a Wine Merchant I have run out near
four hundred pounds & trade not increasing I was very Sensible some way must be thought of to redeem it. My Mind (as You must know) has been always inclined to ye Stage, nay so strongly so that all my Illness & lowness of Spirits was owing to my want of resolution to tell You my thoughts when here, finding at last both my Inclination & Interest required some New way of Life I have chose ye most agreeable to my Self & tho I know You will bee much displeased at Me yet I hope when You shall find that I may have ye genius of an Actor without ye Vices, You will think Less Severe of Me & not be ashamed to own me for a Brother - I am willing to agree to any thing You shall propose about ye Wine, I will take a thorough Survey of ye Vaults & making what You have at Lichd part of ye Stock will either Send You Ire Share or any other way You shall propose - Last Night I played Richard ye Third to ye Surprise of Every Body & as I shall make very near £300 p Annum by It & as it is really what I dote upon I am resolved to pursue it - I believe I shall have Bowers Money which when I have, it shall go towards my part of ye Wine You have at Lichfd pray write me an Answer immediately. I am Dr brother
Yrs Sincerely
D Garrick
I have a farce (Ye Lying Valet) coming out at Drury Lane To Mr Garrick at Lichfield, Staffordshire.
My Dear Brother.

The Uneasiness I have received with Ire Letter is inexpressible; however it was a Shock I expected & had guarded Myself as well as I could against it, and ye Love I sincerely have for You together with ye prevailing Arguments You have made Use of were enough to overthrow My Strongest Resolutions did not Necessity (a very pressing Advocate) on My Side convince me that I am not so much to blame as You Seem to think I am. As to my Uncle Upbraiding You with keeping our Circumstances a Secret I am Surprised at it, for to be Sure What I have run out has been more Owing to my own Willfulness than any Great miscarriage in Trade. but run out I have & let me live never So warily but must run out more, & indeed the Trade we have if You will reflect very seriously can never be Sufficient to Maintain Me & a Servant handsomely - As for ye Stage, I know in ye General it deserves Ire Censure, but if You will consider how handsomely & how reputably Some have lived as Booth Mills Wilks Cibber &c & admitted into, & admired by ye Best Companies; & as My Genius that Way (by ye best Judges) is thought Wonderful how can You be so averse to My proceedings when not only my Inclinations, but My Friends who at first were Surprised at my intent, by seeing me on ye Stage, are now well convinced it was impossible for Me to keep of - As to Company ye Best in Town are desirous of Mine, & I have rec'd more Civilities & favours from Such Since my playing than I ever did in all my Life before; Mr Glover (Leonidas I mean) has been every Night to See me & Sent for Me & told Me As well every Body he converses with, that he had not seen Acting for ten Years before; in Short were I to tell You What they Say about me t'would be too vain tho I am now writing to a Brother - however Dear Peter so willing am I to be continued in ire Affections, that were I certain of a less Income with more reputation I would gladly take to It - I have not yet had my Name in ye Bills & have played only ye Part of Richard ye 3d which brings crowded Audiences every Night & Mr Giffard returns ye Service I have done him very ampley however Dear Peter write me a Letter Next post & I'll give You a full answer not having Time enough at present; I have not a Debt of twenty Shillings upon Me so in that be very Easy. I am Sorry my Sisters are under Such
Uneasiness & as I really love both them & You will ever make it my Study tipper Ire Affect Brothr
D Garrick
To Mr Garrick in Lichfield, Staffordshire.
Dear Brother.

I am very Sorry You still Seem so utterly Averse to What I am so greatly Inclined & to What ye best Judges think I have ye Greatest Genius for - The Great nay incredible Success & approbation I have met with from ye Greatest Persons in England have almost made Me resolve (tho Im sorry to Say it against Ire Entreaties) to pursue it as I certainly shall make a fortune by it, if Health continues - Mr Littleton Mr Pit & Several Other Members of Parliament were to See Me play Chamont in ye Orphan & Mr Pit, who is reckoned ye Greatest Orator in the house of Commons, said I was ye best Actor ye English Stage had produced, & he Sent a Gentleman to Me to let Me know he & ye Other Gentlemen would be glad to See Me - the Prince has heard so great a Character of Me that we are in daily Expectations of his coming to See Me - I have been told that You are Afraid Giffard has had my Money, Upon my honour he does not owe Me a farthing, having paid me long ago what I lent him which was but £30. I receive at present from him (tho tic a Secret) 6 Guineas a Week & am to have a clear Benefit which will be very soon & I have been offered for it £120, You can't imagine what regard I meet with, ye Pit & Boxes are to be put together & I shall have all my friends (who still continue so to Me tho You cannot be brought over) if You come to town ire
Lodgings will cost you Nothing I having a Bed at Arthur's for You, pray let Me know if You'll come immediately & if You choose to have Ire Share with what You have at Lichfield ye Cooper shall take a Strict Survey of ye Vaults & I will be at half ye Expense of ye Carriage, if Not I'll make a Sale here but let Me know what You resolve upon & I will assure You tic my greatest desire to continue Ire affectionate Brothr
D: Garrick
To Mr Garrick at Lichfield, Staffordshire.
London
Tuesday Night
My Dear Brother.

As You finished Ire last Letter with Saying tho you did not approve of ye Stage Yet you would always be my Affect Brother, I may now venture to tell You I am very near quite resolved to be a player; as I have ye Judgment of ye best Judges (Who to a Man are of Opinion) that I shall turn out (nay they Say I am) not only ye Best Trajedian but Comedian in England. I would not say so much to any body else, but as this may Somewhat palliate My Folly you must Excuse me. Mr Littleton was with Me last Night & took Me by ye hand & Said he never saw Such playing upon ye English Stage before - I have great Offers from Fletewood, but he's going to Sell to Gentlemen & I don't doubt but make for myself very greatly - We have greater Business than Either Drury Lane or Covent Garden; Mr Giffard himself Gave Me Yesterday twenty Guineas for a Ticket, & Next Week I design buying £200 pounds of my Stock out of my
Profits of Playing - As to hurting You in Ire Affairs it shall be my constant Endeavours to promote Ire Welfare with my all; If you should want Money & I have it You shall command my whole & I know I shall soon be more able by playing & writing to do You Service than any other Way. I would propose Selling of our Stock here & if You should want more Money than Ire Share will come to, You shall have mine - My Uncle I am told will be reconciled to Me, for even ye Merchants say tic an honour to him not Otherwise, I design if You like it to desire his assistance who by a Lettr from you may be Ire Agent in ye Affair to act in Your Name; You without Doubt will do handsomely there & Get Money - however propose what You please to Me, the Business is rather better than it was, but My Mind is quite turned another way So I desire to be released as soon as possible from it - Enclosed I have Sent you ye Note of Giffard's but can't get it paid, pray send it to Mr Noel for receipt & transact ye Affair & I'll pay you ye Expenses - Write pray immediately
To Mr Garrick at Lichfield, Staffordshire.
Dear Peter.

On Monday last I sent by ye Carrier the Book of Accts & The Lying Valet; the Valet takes prodigiously, & is approved of by Men of
genius & thought ye Most diverting Farce that ever was performed; I believe You'll find it read pretty well, & in performance tic a general Roar from beginning to End; & I have got as much Reputation in ye Character of Sharp & is in any Other Character I have performed tho far different from ye Others. I have at present a cold & hoarseness upon Me & Shall go to Stanmore to Joe Smith to Morrow for a few Days - You perhaps would be glad to know what parts I have played, King Richd - Jack Smatter in Pamela - Clody fop's fortune - Lothario fair Penitent - Chamont Orphan - Ghost Hamlet - & Shall soon be ready in Bays in ye Rehearsal & in ye Part of Othello - Both which I believe will do Me & Giffard great Service - I have had great Success in all, & it is not yet determined whether I play Trajedy or Comedy best - Old Cibber has spoke with ye Greatest Commendation of my Acting. As to playing a Harlequin it is quite false - Yates last Season was taken very ill & was not able to begin ye Entertainment so I put on ye Dress & did 2 or three Scenes for him, but Nobody knew it but him & Giffard; I know it has been Said I played Harlequin at Covent Garden but it is quite false - I should be glad to know what wine You have there & So I can easily tell You what Share of the wine here belongs to You - or else (which I believe would be better) you had better have all that Wine to Yrself & take half of this here, & as you have not Money Sufficient to Undertake it all, draw upon Me & I'll pay it for You & You shall pay Me when You are able. Write Me word immediately ire intention that I may act Accordingly - I am making out ye Bills & will get in ye Money as fast as I can I don't design to bottle of any more wine, but Sell ye rest in Cask. I have received Several very pretty Letters for Mr Newton, ye Clergyman who has been Several Times to See Me - pray is Mr Hassells at Lichfield & what is become of him, he has never writ to Dr Miles his very good Friend, nor has taken any Notice of ye Money he lent him, pray if You See him let him know ye Dr designs to get his Money some way or Other, he owes Me a Small Sum. there is not such a thing as a Seville Orange in Town, there are none but Lisbon crab & they are 3d a piece so I would not Send any - I design to answer Mr Sudal's agreeable Lettr when I return from ye Country pray my best Compliments to him & Family, Love & Service to our Own & believe me ire Sincere Brothr
D: Garrick
To Mr Garrick at Lichfield, Staffordshire.
London
Dear Peter

Ye Two Pipes of Testace's Port will be with You on Saturday - I shall pay Farnell's Bill immediately - I have been very bad of a Cold but am now quite well again & hope I shall continue so; I play Baize next Wednesday for ye first Time - the Success I have met with is incredible, & perhaps what will very much Surprise You, I have Met with as much applause in Fondlewife as in any Thing, so that my General talents that Way are not to be Doubted -

Pamela is wrote by Mr Giffard himself I had no hand in it at all excepting writing ye French Letter which was vastly liked, & tagging ye fourth Act - It is very hungry & was chiefly liked by ye Middling & low Kind of Spectators. You may Assure Anybody It is not of my writing -

Sr Robed is in a very bad hole & I believe He Cant find a Rope strong enough not even in ye Treasury, to draw him out of It - The Patriots talk very much of helping him to one strong enough for his Business another way - Time must Show us with it will come to - Morgan I suppose You have heard is dead - You may have heard too that I am Married, but I will assure You it is false, I believe both of Rank & of Fortune this to YrSelf You may be Sure of ye first intelligence -

My Aunt Fermignac has been with Me & I See my Uncle every Week, I believe a Reconciliation is near at hand - My Lord Essex has sent word Just now he would be glad to See me to Morrow - I guess it must be to Engage me next Season for Rich but I have fixed my Mind upon Drury Lane, tho it is quite a Secret -
I am Dr Br (with usual Loves & Services to ye Family) Ire Affectionate Br
D: Garrick
With is become of Billy pray?

I have sent You two Letters I have received from Mr Lowe & Newton Clergymen, Mr Newton has wrote me Several, I go to Lt Carpenter's Tomorrow - Let me have 'em again pray - To Mr Garrick, Lichfield, Staffordshire.
Dear Peter.

The Night before last I saw Mr Sudall, who with more Lichfield People came to See ye Rehearsal; I have ye Greatest Success imaginable in ye Part of Baize, & instead of clapping Me they hussy which is very uncommon approbation - & tho The Town has been quite tired out with ye Play at ye Other End of ye Town Yet I have ye Great Satisfaction to See crowded Audiences to It Every Night. I never was better in health in my Life & can undergo fatigue like a little Hercules, which makes me of Opinion that Sobriety & regularity will at any time put an Indifferent Constitution upon an Equality with a Good one without those Advantages -
Poor Milward is taken very dangerously ill of a Spotted Fever & given o'er (they Say) by ye Physicians.
Sr Robed Walpole is out of ye Ministry, I am little acquainted with more News of that Sort, the Prince they Say, sees ye King on Sunday next -

I hope ye two Pipes came Safe, I shall send You Two more next Monday & then see with Remains & Know ire Resolution about it - I shall reckon with Wine You have had before from ye Stock as Part of Ire Share of ye Stock, having Sold it among ire Friends there; the Term of ye Vault ends in March, so I must get my Share sold off as soon as possible; Ned's half Year is up ye tenth of March & from that Time I shall look upon him as my Servant Solely.
My Uncle says he'll pay ye Money as desired & wants to know how he shall send ye Bird to You -

Pray let Me Know with I have laid out for You Since You left London, for I have somewhere mislaid ye Acct I kept of 'em - I shall call in ye Debts as soon as possible, then send Ire Acct & As soon as all is finished send You ye Books that You may See there are
no Errors committed. Pray my Love & Services as usual & believe with ye Greatest Affectn
Ire Loving Brothr
D: Garrick
Pray let me Know whether Billy is returned to his Master & reformed?
To Mr Garrick, Lichfield, Staffordshire.
London
April 19th, 1742
Dear Peter.

I have delayed answering Ire Lettr till Mr Jafferies came to Town in Order to Send You ye Snuff: he has not at present any by him but will have in a little Time, & then I will send You Some & pay him according to Order - As to Our Affairs I shall state in a very clear Manner Soon & will get in our Debts as soon as possible. Ned & ye Vault You have nothing to do with from ye 25th of March last -

I have made with Ned an Exact & careful Division of ye wine in my Care here & You have still 2 Hogds of Port one Hogd & half of Madeira & 1 Hogd of Claret taking 6 Dozn, ye Quantity of Claret I sent to You at Lichd for I have reckoned to Your Acct all ye Wine you had at Lichd & we have acted jointly in our Stock here to ye 25th of March 1742 -

My health is better than usual - & the favour I meet with from
ye Greatest Men has made me far from Repenting of my Choice. I Am very intimate with Mr Glover, who will bring out a Trajedy next winter upon My Acct. I have supped Twice with ye Great Mr Murray Councellr & Shall with Mr Pope by his Introduction - I supped with ye Mr Littleton ye Prince's Favourite last Thursday night & Met with ye highest Civility & complaisance, He told me he never knew with Acting was till I appeared & Said I was only born to act with Shakespeare writ, these Things daily occurring give me great Pleasure I dined with Lt Halifax & Lt Sandwich Two very ingenious Noblemen Yesterday & am to dine at Lt Hallifax's next Sunday with Lt Chesterfield, I have ye Pleasure of being very intimate too with Mr Hawkins Brown of Burton, in short I believe nobody (as an Actor) was ever more caressed & My Character as a private Man makes 'em more desirous of my Company - (all this Entry nous as one Brothr to Another) I am not fixed for next Year, but shall certainly be at ye Other End of ye Town - I am offered £500 Guinea & a Clear Benefit or Part of ye Management; I can't be resolved with I shall do till ye Season is finished - As to Mrs Brown Displeasure about ye Places it was their own faults, for I put down ye Box in Mrs Dalton's Name & ye footman asked for Mrs Brown's Box, & I not being there they were disappointed of It; such Blunders of Footmen make the unthinking part of ye world Angry where they should not be - Shall I send Ire remaining Share of ye Wine soon? I will send You our Acct in a very little Time - pray my usual Love & Services to Brothrs & Sisters & I shall ever be theirs & Ire Affete Brothr
D: Garrick
Monday Augt the 19th 1745
Dear Peter.

Yesterday I left Elyzium, & arrived at Hell about 6 o'Clock in ye Evening, blasted with the Wind & drenc'd with ye Rain: The Compy here had expected Me some Time & were very glad to see Me: the most agreeable part left Us this Morning, viz. three Young Ladies with whom I was very merry & happy last Night. Mr Sanford of Lichfield (who knows You) Sets out for Matlock this Day, I think we have no great loss of him: Mrs Brown desires her Service to You all, she is as lively & insignificant as Usual, & for her own Comfort & the Misfortune of her Acquaintance, she has got rantipole Spirits by drinking ye Waters. I never was so pleased with a party of Pleasure in my Life as with that to Tilbury; The Place is one of ye most beautiful I ever Saw, & the Master is a most agreeable Man & not in ye least Shy or cold in his Welcome; had I been better Acquainted with him I should have been quite happy.

Pray my best Affections to Miss Patty Fletcher & desire her not to believe her Sister. If She tells her I am fallen in Love with Miss Vernon; for tho I admire that Young Lady yet My Passion to her is Unalterable & Eternal: & I must desire You to do Your Endeavours to ward of any Blow Miss Molly may design me with her Sister, & if You find her resolved upon my Ruin to bid her (from Me) remember The Ghost in Hamlet . I hope Your Ball goes on Swimingly & that You intend to procure a Haut Boy , to enliven the Dancing; I shall reserve Myself for that Night & I beg You to give my best Compliments to Miss Loveit & Let her know, I shall come on purpose to have ye Pleasure of dancing with her. if I have any Letters on Thursday You must keep 'em for me till I see You; I shall certainly lye at Derby next Sunday Night at the King's Head & if You or Billy or Mr Edmonds or all three will be there in ye Afternoon, I will attend You the next Day to Lichfield by Dinner. I intend waiting upon Mrs Betty Dixey on Sunday in ye Afternoon & drink Tea With her. I am very well & I hope to find You all well & in Spirits in ye Mean time divide My Affections among You & believe me Dear Peter
Yours most Sincerely
D Garrick
I have got a good Bed to Myself & the Entertainments have Exceeded my Expectations -
May 24th 1746
Dear Peter.

Tho I got well to London & was congratulated by all my Friends for my healthy Looks & sleek Countenance, Yet trusting too much to my Spirits & Constitution, I have got a most Severe Cold & Sore Throat attended with a Small Fever; I rambled with Some choice Spirits to Renelaugh Gardens last wednesday Night, & being too thinly clad, & some rain falling, I have suffered ever since for my Imprudence: I have purged, bled & kept my Room & am now scarce able to keep my head up to write to You. I am glad to hear the Linen is come to hand; but Mr Walmisley forgets the Order he gave Me, which I here send you transcribed from his own handwriting: viz. two Dozen of Table Cloths, 2 Yards, half & Nail long;
2 Yds 2n & nail broad for constant use: at 10 or 12s or more a piece as You shall judge : I took care to execute the Commission to ye best of my Power & I hope when ye Goods are looked into, & ye Price known I shall be thought a very careful Steward. I have sent to Ireland for some Linen for Shirts & for some Poplin for my Sisters, they will be with You some time next Month. I have seen Ire Friend Mr Cheap & am to breakfast with him as soon as I go abroad; He is a most agreeable communicative Gentleman & Speaks in a most kind, friendly Manner of You: I intend to ask him to Supper & by that means give My Friends Windham, Draper, &c a feast: he tells Me all his papers are in ye Spaniard's hands, but ye Duke of Bedford insists upon his giving some Account of his rare Adventures from Memory, which will be added, As an Appendix to Admiral Anson's Voyage: there will be a feast for You, & I shall not forget my Promise. Tho I have been ill & much hurried with my own Business; I have consulted my Friends about George: I spoke particularly to my very good Friend Mr Paterson the City Solicitor who told me at once, that He should be in his office as long as he pleased & that he would use him as he would Me; which was so generous an Offer & made with so much friendship & affection, that I desired Drapar to Night at our Club (which I could not attend on account of my Illness) to let him know I should accept of it. Every body says it is ye Most lucky Affair could have happened to him; he'll have an Opportunity of seeing vast variety of Business, & cultivating an Acquaintance (by a proper Behavr) with ye most Amiable, sensible sweet fellow, that ever the Law produced: He can't be there till Midsummer, so let him prepare his affairs & I will send to him when I know more particulars & find things ready for his coming, in ye mean Time let him not be idle. I have given George a Character which I think he deserves & which will infallibly (if he does not deceive me) make him a happy & an Eminent Man: I beg you will talk gravely to him & let him know ye least deviation from ye Idea I have had reason to form of him, must ruin him & if he does not sail Steady & look about him with caution, in this dangerous Sea London, it is right that he should know ye worst & will have this aggravation to his folly (if he should fall) that he was timely forewarned of the Dangers.
My Love & Services attend Sisters & Brothers & Friends My Compliments to Mr Walmisley's Family & I am
Most Sincerely & Affectly Yrs
D Garrick
To Mr Peter Garrick in Lichfield, Staffordshire.
Augst ye 9th 1746
Dear Peter.
I have received ire Three Letters & intended to have answered 'em this Post - the Advertisement you mention in ire last cannot be put into ye Papers;

I can't imagine what whim you have conceived about my hearing Something of ye Situation of Ire Affairs : I will assure You upon My honour, what I wrote was from Myself, & the Result of my best Wishes, Affection & great Brotherly Concern for ire Well-doing; & What I then said, You have often heard me Urge before; but I am sorry I have Spoke my Mind too freely, or that You should Suspect, I either would, or should hear, any thing, from Any Body, to Ire Disreputation or prejudice. If you think Billy has spoke unkindly of You, You do him wrong, great Wrong; for he always
Speaks of you as he ought, & has the greatest opinion of Ire Conduct & Honour: this I will assure You again upon my Word, & it gives me some pain to see You Warm upon Trifles, & suspicious without foundation. I cannot believe You are uneasy, that Billy is willing to know ye State of Family Affairs; it is a laudable & equitable Inquisitiveness; & each individual has an equal Right to his Share in every Transaction,: I am confident You are of the same Opinion & only have been uneasy by drawing Consequences from former Impressions - but no more of this; thus far I thought it my Duty to go, to clear the Innocent & remove unjust prejudices - I have seen a Man, one Sedgwick Mr Victor has got for You; he bears a very good Character, has a very promising Appearance, has lived with Wine Merchants, understands the Business & is willing to live with you for Sixteen pounds a Year, washing & Board; if You agree, he will be with You immediately & You must write the very next post to Billy as You direct to Me, & he will give the Man Ire Answer: He is a very Sober, quiet Young Fellow, & will wait upon You, carry out ire Wine, manage it &c. I go to Cheltnam on Tuesday, so pray write to Billy; if You have any thing to say to Me enclose it & Billy will forward it - the Other Piece of Cloth (You know) Mr Smart desired me to write for; don't you remember? Mr Paterson has lessened his Office of One Clark to make Room for George; he must come up the Beginning of October; I will let him know more Soon & let him not be idle in the mean Time: I have expected an Account of the Particulars of the Mortgage, for I have reserved Money for it, if You will let me into ye State of the Case - My Lord Cromarty will be pardoned & the People murmur Much about it - I have a Print of Richard for Mr Vyse & You; did not I promise him One You shall have it ye first Opportunity - pray my Love & Service to Sisters & George my best Compliments to Mr Walmisley's Family & I am
Dr Peter most Office Yrs
D: Garrick
PS. be sure to write next post for the Man will wait upon Billy for ire Answer don't disappoint him -
Tunbridge Tuesday July 26th 1747
Dear George.

I have drunk ye Waters & they agree with Me - I am taking an Ounce of Bark with them & hope they will Strengthen & recruit Me. There is very good Company here & I have been with them all round - I cannot possibly tell you ye Day I shall return to Town, but I shall give you Notice by a Line - If you write to Me & send any Lettrs I have at home enclosed in a Frank, You must write ye very Night You receive this; for ye Post comes Every Day, & I
shall have it next Thursday - If there is any News or Mr Lacy has any thing to say, let Me know. I go to bed at Eleven, rise at Seven, drink no Malt Liquor, & think of Nothing; which last I am sure has done me more good than any thing Else - remember George to Write To Morrow, (Wednesday night) & remember too, it is a bye Night & you must send ire Lettr to ye Post house Sooner than on ye Other Nights. Old Cibber is here, & very merry we are - Mr Littleton & I are Cup & Can: in short Every body is goodhumoured & for ye time I shall Stay, I shall not rapine or repent ye Expedition - I have played at E: O. & won - I don't dance, but I sleep without my cold Sweats, & Eat like a Ploughman - I write in a very Noisy Coffee house, & having Nothing more to Say
I am thine Dr George, most Affectionately
D. Garrick -
direct for Me at ye Post-house in Tunbridge -
I have opened my Letter again to tell You, that You need not write till Thursday Night if You choose it, for I shall not go from hence till Saturday.
To Mr George Garrick at Barber's Hall in Monckwell Street near Aldersgate, London.
Bath March 31st 1751
Dear George.

We got here Friday Evening by Seven o'Clock; Ire Sister was much jolted for ye ten last Miles, & bad Roads they are, tho not dangerous - the Moment you have ye least intelligence when we open at ye Playhouse let me know, for if we don't begin Easter Monday, I will drink ye waters, for my Stomach is not in ye best Order - pray call now & then in Southampton Street, & look into ye Stables & see if Robin is Neat & tight & takes care of things, I believe he is honest, but he has a great Trust, & a wary Eye will not be amiss - a word to ye wise - now for Ire own Affair - I must beseech You to look narrowly into things & be sure of Matters before you Engage - Your Whole depends upon it, & should You be deceived (I only say should you) You will be certainly worse than You are, & Miserable, therefore I say, take Heed; but when You are well assured of Your Point, & You like ye Party, It will prove a very lucky incident of ire Life. however if You consult with ye Good friend Mr Squire, You cannot Err in one part, & if you consult Ire own Heart, & find it willing, in ye Other, You maybe a very happy Man -.
I have drawn You out a Letter which You may alter, or omit parts of it, as will best suit with ye Circumstances of ye Affair -
Madam.

Tho I have not ye Pleasure of knowing You but by Sight, yet from that little Knowledge of You, I have often wished for more; I could not help making this Declaration to Mr - who has most kindly
offered me his assistance to introduce me to ire acquaintance; I am most Sincerely obliged to him, but how I can make my Excuses to You, for desiring him to use his Interest for Me, gives me great Perplexity; for if you should think Me in ye least wanting in Respect by this abrupt manner of addressing You, I should be as much mortified with that, as I should receive pleasure in knowing that my Friends Good offices on my behalf were not unsuccessful. all I shall urge in my own Justification, is ye well meaning intention of my heart; & if the truest Esteem for ire Person & Character, may entitle me to ire favourable interpretation, I may hope that this Letter may be received without Offence, & that I may have the Satisfaction of thanking You for such a Reception in Person.
I am Madm Ire most Obedt humble Sert If my proposal would not be thought too importunate, I could wish to have Ire leave, to desire Ire Mama's permission, that I may wait upon You Some Day this Week.
Now Dr George, let me desire You for Ire own Sake to Enquire into her Character & that of Ire friend; You cannot be too circumspect in this grand affair of ire Life -
March 21st, 1752
Dear Peter.

I am glad You & Company got safe to Your dear beloved Lichfield, & as glad that You found all well at ye Castle on ye Bridge. You need not have troubled Mr Sharpless to frank Ire Letters, for notwithstanding his Name we were obliged to pay Eight pence for it. I believe he has no right to frank any but his own Letters, and therefore you should Send nothing sent; for ye future trouble not ire Self for such kind of Trifles, will frank and send Any thing of yours for me at a small Sum - I must desire You to Enquire immediately in ye Bishop's Court, what Legacies Lady Avery left & to whom, her Will I suppose is deposited there, & she died about 3 Years ago. these are my Lt Hartington's Com~ands & I beg you'll execute 'Em directly. was it not a £50 Bank Note I gave You? such I intended it; the Reason of my asking is, that I had another in my Pocket Book & am not quite certain if I gave you ye right - must I bottle off ye Ale when it is fine, or what must I do with it besides making myself & friends merry? pray my best Respects to Mr Smart & Mr Seward. pray do not forget Mine & my Wife's Compts to ire Neighbor Mr Fletcher, we talk of him often - our best Loves to Sisters & Ire self
& I am most sincerely & Affectionately thine
D. Garrick
P.S. The felons in Newgate I hear last Night rose against ye Keepers & have murdered some. I don't know ye Particulars.
May ye 12th 1752
Dear Peter.

My Wife has spoken to Lord Hartington & in ye Strongest Terms upon Your Letter & Recommendation: His Lordship told her that he would certainly write & he should be very glad to serve this Friend of Yours, with several other Compliments too tedious here to mention , as ye Show Bills say.

I shall immediately when I have finished our theatrical Campaign, & settled ye Company, determine about ye £400, & send you word - this is our last Night of acting this Season. I have sent you ye Empty Cask, we have not yet tasted our ale, as we imagine it not yet quite fit to make merry with. You promised Me before you left London, to send me My Age as it is written in ye Old Bible, with ye Erasement & interlineation, I shd likewise be glad that Sister Linney would send her Judgment upon ye matter, & as I believe she can have no particular reason to conceal her age no more than Myself, I beg she would Speak without favour to Either.

George has had a bad cold, but is better, his wife is well - Draper is returned from Bath as bad as he went, I have lent him a Horse for his last resort, but I think the machine is too far gone to be repaired - My wife sends her Love to you all & I am
most Sincerely & affecty yours & their's
D: Garrick
To Mr Garrick at Lichfield, Staffordshire.
Chiswick
June 12th 1752?
Dear Peter.

Had there been any particular Business in ire last Letter to Me, I should certainly have answered it directly; but the finishing of ye Season, ye hurry of New Engagements, & all backed with ye damn'dest Cold that Ever made a poor Mortal Snuffle, have rendered me quite incapable of Every thing, but Signing my Name to Articles, & blowing my Nose; with ye latter of which, I have filled no less than four Hankerchiefs a Day - I am sorry to hear Sister Linney is so bad - I Could have wished that I had known it sooner, for I really think her Health should have been first considered before I have consulted many of my Physical friends about her; have told 'Em of ye Redness of her Face, & that we believe her case to be scorbutic - they think Scarborough would do well - but they think Cheltenham as well, & in some Cases better - & they say Cheltenham Water is so little altered by Carriage that if she liked it she might drink it at home - if you will send me ye Particulars of her case, I will advise with ye best, & send yo their Opinions - she must Eat very little Meat, & no salt Meat; I cannot tell how she lives in general, but I desire you would let me know - if they shd advise ye Cheltenham Waters, let her be regular with them & they must do her good by all acct. If they don't do all we Expect; I shall desire she may go ye Next Season to Scarborough, but I think ye Nearest & Easiest Remedy shd be tried first - write to me directly & you shall receive my answer for I am going to Yorkshire in a fortnight Merrial is with George, so I can give no Account of her, not having seen her for this last Week - I must desire you once more to send a Copy of my age, as it stands exactly in ye Bible with ye razure & interlineation; am not I Seven & thirty, or only Six ye last birth day? - My Love to Sister & believe Me
Most affecty Yours & her's
D Garrick
pray write ye next post
Dear George.

I hope before this that You & Spouse are well & quietly settled in Ire new habitation - When ye Dressing Room is finished Send me ye Bills & I'll send you ye Money - let it be pretty & worthy of my reception or tell Siss that I shall throw her & her dressing Room into ye Attorney General's Gardens.

What News from ye profound Lacy? I will not give above Seven Pounds p. Week to Bland , & so far You may answer for me, if there is occasion. pray is there any hopes of Draper's recovery? is there any pain in ye Operation of Tapping? does it make ye Patient faint? how does Mrs Draper bear it? - pray remember Me to Kent and tell him that had I any thing to tell him that could divert him, I had written to him before, but what signifies troubling him for Nothing - if this does not satisfy him, let him know I will copy out a Letter from Wit's common wealth & send it to him by ye next post. What say ye Town about Messrs Taaff & Montagu's affair? Lady Burl: is obliged to you for ye Care of her Orders to ye Porter - When does Clutterbuck return to Town, does he know of Lacy's agreement with Maddox - I fancy Lacy will Exhibit him in ye little house in ye Hay market - With all my heart - anywhere so he does not pollute ye purity of Drury Lane -

I hope Saunders is getting ye New Entertainment forward, for I would have it ready as soon as possible. is Woodward returned from Birmingham? My Love to him when You see him & thank him for ye Cloak bag - tell him that I hope he will take care to have good houses at ye Opening - till I come -
Love to ye Lass with her round Waste, & believe Me
Thy most Affect Brothr
D: Garrick -
pray how does My Wife's Maid Nanny, is She better than when We left her, ask her & Send me Word.
Tuesday Augst 25th 1752
Dr George

I have Enclosed a Letter for Clutterbuck which I desire You'll let him have immediately, I have left ye Rose Tavern affair to Him & You - do as You think proper & I shall be satisfied. I hope by this You have fathomed ye Dirty Heart of my Partner, I expect to hear Something of Him by ye next post -

You mention in ire Lettr to Me the famous Peter Wood , he may be famous for ought I know, but ye Devil take me if Ever I heard his Name before - I hope if ye Rose is taken by Us, that we shall behave handsomely to Miles , for I think he did so by Us -

I could wish that You would take a ride to Ealing & inspect ye house & premises You Mention; by ire Description it must fit Me; I hope it wont be gone before I can see it with my Wife; pray send me ye particulars of it, has it any prospect? I desire You will thank
Mr Carrington for his kind Care of Me in this affair - Saunders would be a good Man to take with You to see ye house, he will know ye Condition of it at once -

I have not answered Leviez's Letter because I imagine he will be in London before one can reach him - Devise I find is coming over, & I hope that he won't bring Pitro too, however we must stand ye Chance; if he shd send a Lettr, open it, & if he sends to know whether we want Pitro with Devise , I think not, our Company is over loaded already, thanks to my Partner Timbertop . I hope Robin will get ready to set out for Us with ye Chariot & four & a Postilion, this Day Sen'night Tuesday ye 1st of Sepbr, he must go to Lincoln & from thence to ye water Side at a place called Wintringham & stay there till we come to him on Friday - He will go there in four Days Easily, pray desire him not to hurry ye horses, & let nobody ride in the Chariot - remember to tell him this - & let him bring with him a Play of Every Man in his Humour & Romeo & Juliet , you may have both from Draper . I shall let You know in my next how You may write to Me on ye Road for I want to know how ye Opening will be & other Matters - I don't think so ill of Moore's play as You do, nor so Well of it as Draper - but mum . I hope when we return that we shall find You & your good wife well - give her a kiss for us both & believe Me
Ire most affect Brother
D Garrick.
The Reason I shall want ye two Plays Every Man , & Romeo , is that I would read 'Em upon ye Road to be ready at a Moment's Warning.
Let Cross have ye Enclosed wherever he is, read it & seal it up -
Augst 28th 1752
My Dear George.

I hope Robin is set out for Us, & that You have given him directions in writing, If he is not yet gone, for I am not sure whether I ordered him Monday or Tuesday send him forth the Morning after you receive this, which will be Tuesday Sepbr 1st & write the same Night to Me, here as usual, & I shall receive it time enough to go from hence to meet him at ye Water Side Either Friday or Saturday - but I hope Your next Letter will clear up that to Me & then I shall not be kept in Suspense. however George, write me a few Lines on Tuesday, & I shall be more certain, for we receive ye Letters by six in ye Morng & We may set out on our Journey after that - I hope Robin has directions to go to Wintringham by ye Ombre side & wait there for Us - His Journey shd be as follows - from Londn to Biggleswade from Begged to Stamford , from Stamd to Lincoln & from Linn to Wintringham , which last is a very easy day's Journey - however let him do What he will, so he comes safe & well to Wintringham & there wait for Us - If You should write me a Letter ye Night the house Opens Saturdy ye 16th direct it for Me to be left at the Swan at Wellwyn in Hertfordshire where I must stop half a Day to settle Matters with Dr Young - pray write to me there with an acct of ye house, ye Play & other Matters I think you are right to Soften the
rough places, which I had put in for Lacy, I want to know much how ye portion works with him - let me know the particulars - Yates is an unaccountable Dog, & I'm afraid has kicked down all ye Milk at Birmingham. My best Services to Woodward & thank him for his News about Theo Cib: but sure it cannot be - pray tell Would I have some News for him too. Miss Auretti, MonSr Pitro, Madme Janeton, ye Father, Mother & all their Generation may Kiss my A-se; I am so sick of their no meaning Messages & Compliments, that Every time I see her Name in a Letter, my Stomach falls a heaving as Yours would do, if You were to sit with Your Nose over a Pot with a Stale Turd in it, & that turd not ire own - No more of ye Aurettis I beg you - heugh - is there any talk of Rich's Opening? when? & who has he got. Say Nothing of Dr Young's play - I have doctored Moore's a little, that is - thickened ye Pudding a little, for indeed as ye Taste of ye Audiences is at present, it was too much upon ye Squatter for 'Em - I can write no more, & I have so laughed with writing this Nonsense that Im but just able to send Love to little Siss
Yrs Ever & Ever
D G -
Tuesday Sepbr 1st, 1752
Dear George.

I received by this Post a Letter from my friend Clutterbuck & You - I find by his, that Lacy has been with him, & is almost dead with
ye bloody Flux - He ought to have a thorough Scouring before his inside will be tolerably clear from ye filth & Nastiness that he has been gathering from his Youth upward till now - He desires me to forgive him; that I will with all my heart for I thank my God that I have no Malice in my Nature, but I can't forget him soon, nor will I be upon Brotherly terms with him; there is a rank viciousness in his Disposition that can only be kept under by ye Whip & curb - I suppose Robin Set out for Us this Morng & that he will be at Wintringham on Friday Night - We propose leaving this place Saturday Morng & hope to see You about Wednesday; for as I told You before I must have some Conversation with Dr Young - but say Nothing of this to Lacy, & if he asks when I shall come, say You can't tell - My Service to Cross & let him know I have received his last Lettr & I shall be very well contented with what is Settled, till I see him - Mr Woodward must choose which part he will do in ye Silent Woman & I think Shutter will do Daw as well as any thing - tell him yt I suppose Mr Lacy will Settle ye Parts in ye Double Disappoint - to ye best advantage - I hope he has spoke to Mossop about Subtle - If You write to me a Line about ye house On Saturday Night (ye Opening), direct for Me at ye Bell at Stilton in Huntingtonshire to be left till called for, & for fear of ye worst put in another at ye Same time (two lines will do) directed for Me at ye White Swan at Wellwyn in Hertfordshire to be left till called for, they will neither Miscarry for I know both ye Landlords, & they will carry ye Letter barefoot into Scotland, rather than I should not have it - My Wife thinks ye Maids have Mistook her about cleaning ye windows, She meant that the Glazier was to do 'Em as Usual, & hopes that they have not been showing their Ars-s out of ye windows in Order to clean 'Em - I long to see ye house at Ealing, I am prepossessed that it will do - Mr Carrington is very Obliging, & I shall tell him so when I see him - I am glad to hear that Siss keeps so well, I suppose there will be no Seeing her face for her Belly when I come to Town - give our kindest & best Love to her & both of You believe
Me Ire most affect Brother
D: Garrick -
I have thought better of it, You may if you please only write to Stilton , I have sent you franks.

I have Enclosed You half a dozen Lines upon ye affair between Withers & my friend Dr Garnier , if you like 'Em put 'Em into ye
Penny post sealed up, the Publisher of ye Whitehall I dare say will put 'Em in, if not there will be no great loss - say Nothing of 'Em to anybody, be sure -
Adieu!
My Wife desires you'll bid ye Maids dust ye red Room & Pictures, but to care of Gilding & Carving.
Chiswick
July ye 4th 1753?
Dear Peter

I have just now heard that there is an Estate belonging to one Mr Boothby (I don't know if it is Ire friend or not) near Ashbourn, of about £300 p ann to be sold, & has been upon Sale near Two Years - Dr Taylor ye Physician tells me that it is one of ye prettiest
freehold Estates in ye County of Derby - I wish you would make some Enquiry about it, & let me know ye particulars as soon as You can - pray inform Me if there is ye River Dove near ye house, & what kind of a house, what Wood, what prospect &c &c? - I should be glad to purchase a Good thing in Derbyshire, that I might serve ye Devonshire family upon Occasions. I could be glad that you would get ye best information you can, but not mention my Name Yet, for fear they should rise upon it - Mr Fletcher would perhaps give some account of it - Dr Taylor ye Clergyman who lived once at Ashbourn & belongs now to Westminster told my friend Dr Taylor ye Physician of it - They say it is ye prettiest thing next to Mr Oakover's in ye County - I own I love a good Situation prodigiously, & I think the four great Requisites to make one are, Wood, Water, Extent, & inequality of Ground - I should be glad to know if this place has any, or all - shd you hear of any good thing besides this, that may be had reasonably, & has taste in it, (for do you mind Me, there must be a little Taste for Us), I beg you will let me know - but first Enquire about this Estate of Mr Boothby, I think they say The River Dove washes his Land; which would be a great Inducement to Me, for I must have a River - I am writing now in ye greatest haste, & with ye damndest pen I ever handled; but, you'll decipher me, I don't doubt - I imagine we shall go for Yorkshire on Monday; when You write to me direct for Me under Cover to ye Earl of Burlington in Piccadilly London My wife sends her Love with Mine to you all, & believe Me -
Most Affecty & Sincerely Yrs
D Garrick
how does Linney do?
To Mr Garrick in Lichfield, Staffordshire.
Sir.

You were most Extremely Welcome to the Ticket or any other assistance in My Power in all your Undertakings, whether Serious or Whimsical - If you choose to relinquish Your right to ye freedom of Drury-Lane Playhouse, you certainly will do as you please - but without ye Ticket, I imagine Mr Murphy will find the Doors open to him as usual - and be it farther known to You Sir, that as I thought You were above an undue Influence, I never meant ye Ticked as ye least Tie upon The Liberty of Your Pen or Conversation. The Mistake between Us about ye Young Apprentice , is indeed most Mysterious & Surprising, & as it was impossible to give you any
promise for this Season, on account of my other Engagements with Mr Foot &c, so I most Solemnly declare, that (however You may have mistaken Me) I never hinted or thought of performing it this Winter; nay I imagined You were quite Satisfied with It's appearing next Year, at ye beginning of ye Season, that you approved of It's being left with Me for alterations, (if necessary), & that at ye Same time I told You in what Manner I would Endeavour to Strengthen ye Author's Night. but Supposing this Mistake between Us about ye Time of It's appearing; how could it be insinuated to ire disadvantage that I refused Ire Piece? so far from that - have I not said Every where & to Every body who knew Us both, that ye Subject was well imagined & that I would Act & do Every thing in My Power to make it succeed? - I assure You that I desire no Gentleman to wait upon Me unnecessarily, I hope that I give Myself no Unreasonable Airs to any Author, & however I may have been Misrepresented, I flatter Myself that No Gentleman who has had Dealings with Me, will do me the injustice to charge Me with breach of Promise, false Parade, or the Want of Warmth to Support their Performances, in my double Capacity of Manager & Actor.
I am Sr Ire most Obedt hume Served
D Garrick.
P.S. I was obliged to go from Home Yesterday the moment I had dressed Myself, or I should have sent You an answer before -
Hampton Sepbr 2d 1754?
Dear Peter
