S. has sorely vexed me; I always thought she had a foolish liking for ye Drama, & ye dramatis personae , but I could not have imagined, yt the flesh with have overpowered her Spirit, when there was a good understanding to have helped in the Struggle - it is a most deplorable Business indeed! Lord & Lady Spencer left us more than a fortnight ago, & my Pleasures & Spirits are gone with them, his Lordp has made no great purchases in virtue` - he is in treaty about ye famous Magdalen of Guido in ye Barberini Palace at Rome, & I believe he will succeed. He has bought two very famous pictures of Salvator Rosa at florence, & gave two hundred pounds less than ye late Lord Leicester once offered for them; these & a famous Ring, which was Prince Eugene's, & bought of Count Zanetti at Venice, are all his treasure from Italy: I forgot a woman's head by
Raphael, as they say, & a very good Sketch of a Picture by Baroche. We lived in the same house with Mr Howard & Mr Langdale - I think it was lucky they travelled together - the first is a very worthy good natured Young Man, & I don't know a better Sort of Man than the last - He is prudent & sensible & what he wants in learning is better supplied by discretion & an Understanding in Spite of his bigotry - I'll answer for it, that Norfolk House is not mistaken in him. Your Grace's trouble, & my Impertinence is at an End -
Mrs Garrick joins with me in Duty to your Grace & in Respects to Lady Dorothy & all the Lords.
I am Your Grace's Most faithful humble Servant
D Garrick
PS. We Expect to be in England ye beginning or rather ye 2d Week in August - we shall go by Ausburgh, Stratsburgh, Nancy &c -
Munich the Capital of Bavaria
Augst the 23d 1764
My dear George

My wife wrote to You when I was upon my sick bed, but recovering, I now write myself, to free You from all fears of Me , as Yours dated the 12th of July has Me, of You - I have had a most violent bout of it
indeed, but by Care, I am told my health will be ye better for it - our Disorders are partly of ye same kind, & tho we suffer much in our Sickness (I almost gave myself up for gone) we are ye better for it afterwards - I desire no more of this purification - I had two Physicians - I have often made Myself happy that You could Enjoy Hampton tho I could not, I hope You have had ire family there, sent for the Cows, had the old Mare, rid about, Eat ye best fruit, & got Yrself stout as a Lion again to go throe ye next Campaign, pray go often to Hampton & do, as if it was your own.

I think we had a narrow Escape from ye fire tho Your great & brotherly attention to my Concerns there did You no good. for God's sake, my dear George, why will You say I love to hurt You, whenever I receive a letter from You such Expressions damp ye great pleasure I have in receiving it, & particularly as I am now - You might have seen by my letter yt I wanted to come off my not mentioning Coley's Girl in my Letters, & therefore, if I remember right so foolish a thing, I said I wondered you had not delivered my Compts there, & this was all - but for God's sake my dear George don't let Us be warm upon such Nonsense, we love Each other Much, confide in Each Other, & have so many other things of Consequence to think upon, that I beg you'll never mistake me again & hurt me - by ye bye I don't like ye wench, & never thought of her, & yet I would not offend Colman, who I fear will be much harassed with her - an Idiot - my Friend Colman's Fortune & Expectations have made me happy, what a happy little Rogue it will be! - I am sorry ye trumpery cost duty & surprised about ye few books for they all came from England, & most of 'Em, English - I have hired no dancers, I am in treaty for a pair for next Year, if you had written ire Wants Sooner, I could have got a very active Girl at Padua. I shall certainly follow Your & My Friends Advice about not Acting - ire Judgment coincides so much with my own, that it is resolved - the Music you receive may be kept apart till I come - let Johnson have ye Vols - I am a little at a loss what You will do for a Woman Tragedian to stare & tremble with ire Heroes, if Yates should bitch You - but she must come. I hope that Powel will continue to please - He must have a Master to watch his English which I suppose Coley will do - how do Holland & He (Powel) agree - Jealous - Clive I suppose more Fussocky than Ever, & Pritchard often ailing - Pope I hope flourishes - Pray let me know if You think of ye Invasion next Year - or do you keep it till I can oversee it Myself -

What is become of Hardham's Girl? & of Jack himself? I could wish by ye bye that You would Ask Leach if he has paid ye 100 pts to Jack I am security for - I am sure you have looked a little into my affairs at Hampton & that all is round & sound - I wish I could part with ye manor of Hendon . I am afraid Mrs Wyld is asleep - if that Weight was off my heart, it would be lighter - but some lucky time may come - My Love to Clutterbuck & all all friends from one End to the Other -
I can scarce hold my pen in my hand - direct to Me a MonSr MonSr G chez Monsieur Sager Munck a Franckfort - write directly, & take care to put it into ye proper post -
My dearest Brother, Your most truly & Affectionately
D Garrick
PS. I have wrote about poor Linney several times. Angleterre , To George Garrick Esqr in Somerset Stable Yard in the Strand, London.
Paris
Dear Colman.

You see by ye Enclosed that you will have a letter by ye next post - when ye Baronet sends it, I shall direct it only, & put it into ye post - I have desired to see him, for it was much ado that we knew how to send ye letter, but he keeps with ye lady, & sees No body chez lui - I'll go to ye Ambassador's tomorrow in hopes of catching him, & I will call at Mademlle Clair's for that purpose too; but I am sorry that you did not draw upon him in my favour (as ye Trade calls it) & then I shd have had a sort of right to torment him - he has some ready money at present, & I could wish that we had our 150 out of it - Monsr de Beaumont wants to know what Security you have,
& he can tell you what is to be done here - tho if you are safe in Ireland what more can be done about ye great debt?

My dear Colman you frightened with me ye Extract of a Lettr from Paris - I am very sorry that you mentioned ye woeful want of me as Managr & Actr - they will suspect it came from me, & I have no right to say so much, as I have been taking my pleasures & left ye Theatre for a time - it appears ungenerous & ungrateful in me: which hurt me much - I beg that you will do all you can to make them not think ye paragraph mine, if I am suspected - I never in my life praised myself knowingly except a little matter in ye Fribbleriad , which always pinched me - perhaps I am too sensible about this delicacy, & nobody thinks about me or ye Extract - settle my mind about that matter in ire next - the devil was in you to mention the hoop at Sadler's Wells , for I wrote that very thing to my Friend Arden at Lord Sponsor's - I desired you to say something against me, & you stuck ire Pen in ire heart, & wrote as you felt - I wish from my Soul that you had not - If Becket mentions you to any body, it is just as as bad - Made Riccoboni (a very good Novelist, & a generous Creature,) is very angry with Becket. I took his part - I fear he did not do right, she is much hurt at him - We had a fine laugh at Baron D'Albach's (where you dined once) about the Wicked Compy I keep; I am always with that Set. pray set my Mind at Ease, I hate to be thought malicious -

Has George said any thing to you about it - ? pray tell me for I can't know Elsewhere, with is become of Hardham's Girl ? & tell me what Poem is that against Murphy & others - there is likewise a Vole of Poetry with cuts & very pretty head & tail pieces I saw in Suard's hands pray let me know something about these matters
Yrs ever & cordially
D G.
Love to yrs
P.S. vive la Clandestine Marriage!
Paris March 10th 1765
My dear Colman.

I can very readily believe what You tell me of my Brother Consul - He will never forgive my being the means of his making a figure in the world - but this between Ourselves. I have other matters for You when I see You, & which he does not expect - but Mum - pray does Powell continue to visit you, & get a little Sense from you, or is he topsy turvey like ye rest & thinks like Ricd ye 3d that he is himself alone ? I hope he is wiser - but I'll answer for Nothing or Nobody in a playhouse - the Devil has put his hoof into it, & he was a Deceiver from ye beginning of ye world - tell me really what you think of him - I am told by several that he will bawl & roar - Ross , I hear, has got reputation in Lear - I don't doubt it - the Town is a facetious Gentleman - What do you mean, my good friend, by my being obliged to appear, if I manage? upon looking over ire letter, I find your words are Expected to appear - I must entreat you to be very sincere with me - do the Town in general really wish to see me on ye Stage? or are they (which I rather think ye truth) as cool about it as their humble Servant? - I have no maw for it at all, & yet something must be done to restore our credit: that I may be able to play, & as well as Ever, I will not deny, but that I am able to do as I have done, wear & tear, I neither must or can, or will - the Physicians here, Dr Gem among the rest, advise me, to a man, against appearing again - I had a little nervous attack last week, & the Dr croakt more hoarse than usual against my thinking to do as formerly. Tranquillity & retiremt from business (he says) are the only means to make me Myself again. a Tragedy here called ye Siege of Calais written by a Friend of ye Clairon & also my intimate, has made ye People Mad. The Boxes from top to bottom are all taken for Months to come - they give it gratis next Wednesday to ye People, when ye Doors will be opened at 12 o'Clock at Noon, & the Play will begin at 2. it is ye present Epidemical distemper - The Author has recd many favours from ye King - 3000 livers - a Gold Medal - Liberty to dedicate to him - and with not - the French will hardly bear to hear a Criticism upon it - the following distich is handed about in terrorem .

D'un Auteur Citoyen vouloir ternir l'honneur, C'est pretendre a l'Esprit au depens de son Coeur.
however there are some objections made by ye cooler few - there is much merit in ye Play, & more luck in ye Choice of the Subject - I rejoice at the success, for Monsr de Belloy the Author of it is a most ingenious Modest & deserving man - his Genius is an honour to his own Country & would be to any other - You may mention something of this in ye St James's but not from Me - now to serious business we'll advance -

I cannot get a Meeting with ye Chevalier - he is never at home & has not yet appointed a Meeting with me. I send you the last letter I had from him - I would have you write directly to him & before I set off, I will endeavour to get ye draught accepted, for our Friend de Beaumont advises that - I will certainly have a categorical answer from him, which may force him to acceptance & then I will leave ye Note in good hands to get ye money by force. I had a consultation with Mr Beaumont & another Lawyer, they both thought the getting the bill accepd ye best way - ire Indemnification must pass ire common Pleas (you know how) before we could ask a permission here to execute it upon Sr H. a round about way, but might be done - the method in hand is ye best, cd we but get him to Accept. I have sent you a Copy of my lettr (Copied by my Italian Served) when I sent ye Note (for I could not see him) & his answer - You must press the Acceptance, & say, that you shall make a bad figure with me, that I have laid out money for You, & in my next to him, I shall desire an Answer in a very plain manner & hint that you have not used me well to send me a draught was doubtful of acceptance - if you like this Scheme, let me know directly - for I shall have but just time to do it, as it shd be done - I shall follow ire directions. this is all I can say at present, for ye boy waits to take it to our Ambassador's - it goes by his bag -
Yrs Ever & most truly
D Garrick
Madam sends her best to you mine to yrs
A Gentleman Yesterday showed me a letter from England in which was ye follg lines to me have they been in ye Papers?
I have not got it right the third line is better in ye Original but I have not time to recollect it -
June 30th 1766
Dear Colman.

I rejoice much at your safe arrival at Paris - You set out in Storm & tempest & we were afraid that the Sea would have been rather too frisky for ire Stomachs - but the worst is past, & I hope madam & You are well contented with Leviez & his accommodations. to begin with what you are most interested about, I must tell, that ire sweet boy is at this instant as happy & as well as Ever I knew him - I have made him two visits since ire departure, which he has taken most kindly - the last time his Eyes sparkled when he saw Me - He is greatly desirous to know why I call him Georgy go ging - & has very seriously interrogated his Duenna about it - We have worked very hard in the Garden together, & have played at Ninepins till I was obliged to declare off - He is well taken care of indeed - the old Lady, & the maiden Pierce, are most trusty Guardians, & be assured that you may set ire tender hearts at rest about him - I go to Essex tomorrow, & at my return, We are to have a day at Hampton, & he is to make love to my niece Kitty, & a plumb-pudding - He seems very fond of ye Party, & we will endeavour to make him forget his loving parents - once more my dear friend, Let not a single thought about ire Boy disquiet You - He could not be better if you were with him - so no more of that. Thompson dined with me at Hampton - he spoke very highly & affecty of You - he has no design upon us this next Season, but talks of trying his hand again - he intends writing to you, I believe him to be a very good natured, wellmeaning Man - Steevens has inquired after me to give me some papers from You - what they are I can't tell, but we have missed one another, & I am still in ye Dark; & you don't mention with they are in ire letter -
I have had a letter from Bickerstaff, he is at Paris, & is going to give some Account of our Theatre in the Journal Encyclopiq : You will see it I suppose -

Sanderson tells Me that they have laid ye timbers for ye first floor of ire house, it rises most magnificently to the Ferry-Passengers; you'll be surprised to find yrself Master of a Chateau at ire return - don't lose the Autumn for planting trees to screen you from timber Yard - my love to Madam & remember me to Leviez - You must not see a single french friend of Mine, but you must tell him,
how much I am his humble Servant - God bless you & believe me
most affectionately yrs
D Garrick
George desires his best to you
A Monsieur, Monsieur Colman chez Monsr Leviez, Merchant des Estampes, rue des Arcs, Fouxbourgs St Germains A Paris.
Sir.

Mr King's Accident & Mrs Yates's Indisposition have distressed our affairs so much, that we shall really want Matter to go on with ye business of ye theatre, if we don't bring out what we have in Rehearsal without them - besides if we defer the Alteration of ye Country Wife, we shall not be able to fulfil our Engagements with other Authors - The parts of our Play were delivered out as fast as they were written, & Mr Dodd & Miss Pope who have long Characters (particularly Dodd) had not theirs till the time You favoured me with ire first letter, so I cannot imagine where the Gentlemen of ye other house got their Intelligence. I am very glad that You have not ye least Care about it, but the Whip-hand must be Yours from the Novelty, & Variety - I cannot say that I agree with You in not caring, whether they are damned, or not, I wish 'Em both Success, & don't doubt but they Will have it.
I am Sir your most humble Served
D: Garrick
Sunday
My dear Coley.

Hampton has had a prodigious Effect upon Me: my Cough & hoarseness are 50 p cent better for ye Change of air - instead of coughing all night, I have been disturbed but twice & thrice & that not rudely, & have passed ye rest of ye Night very pleasantly -

My Wife has persuad'd Me to stay here till Wadi when I hope to wait upon the English Merchant with all my wits & Spirits about Me - in ye meantime, I could wish, if not disagreeable to You, that You would look in upon them on Wednesday , & I will make my appearance on Thursday Morning: I hope to see You Wadi Evening : my Wife says if you will dine with us on Wadi at four She will present us with a fine haunch of Venison - Say You will , in a Note by ye Bearer to Morrow - You must write to me; & say if I am to furnish an Epilogue for the Merchant - I certainly will do my best if you are not provid'd -
If you intend to stand by ye London Journal, I will prepare some comicality for it; I have a hundred thoughts about it, & will be always doing something.

I intend Crambo to be ye laughing Rhyming reviewer of Every thing - Mrs Pritchard has sent a most kind Message to Me, & will do anything I desire her - she shall set the Part agoing, & when we are safe landed (tho if Mrs Bennet played it there is not ye least danger) Mrs Hopkins may Relieve her, in case of Indisposition &c &c - Poor Becket is very angry with Baldwin for abusing What we act, & he prints - pray keep up ye Ball, we shall have some sport with him.
My Love & Best Services to Madam & kiss to your dear little Boy, & my warmest Affections to Your Self my dear Coley -
D: Garrick.
Sunday Apple 5th 1767
My dear George.
In the first place, I am grown as fat as a Hog & You may measure with Me at my return to London, without tucking in Your Guts, till Your face is as red, as bull-beef.

I have had a letter from Never who is at Paris, & offers us his Service, in preference to the Opera , Vienna & other Engagements he may have - if Mr Lacy has altered his Mind, I will write to know his proposals; if Mr Lacy thinks it not right to have him, I will let him know we are Engaged - Send me a line about that on Tuesday Post or Wednesday's at farthest, for I will send you a french letter to be put into ye Post on Tuesday afterwds.

Colman & Changuion are arrived - We pulled off our hats, but did not smile - our Friends here will stir heaven & Earth to bring Us together - make ye best of it, it will be but a darn. and does Dido please? Good God! - & will they come twice to see it? - Good God! it is time to leave ye Stage, if such a performance can Stand upon It's legs: - Good God! -

I have seen a paragraph for Cautherly but not an Advertisement - I hope ye Lad will get Something - I expect a full Account, (& hope of a full house at King's Benefit), of the New hodge podge of Linco: pray let me know it by ye first post; that will be on Tuesday , ye day you receive this -

Have you seen Kelly yet? - do you know any thing of his play? - Is Johnston yet arrived from Ireland? - I believe Arthur would gladly receive Miss Reynolds? - I have told him that I with give Up her Articles to her advantage - he knows what she has, & has dined with Mr Davenport - so that perhaps she with be as willing to part with
us, as We with Her. Suppose You were to feel her pulse on this Matter, I have kept up her Importance with Arthur - they ask for her here much, & indeed she would be right to desire her Conge` of Us - I see advertised ye theatrical Campaign price s1-d6 - have you heard of it? - pray let me know what the Subject is, & what they say of it? Love to Your dear little ones -
Ever & most affectionately Yours
D: Garrick
Poor Jacob Tonson -

I have not put ye name of ye Inn on Dr Hawkesworth's letter, for I doubt whether it is Lion's or Clement's , I believe it is ye last, if Johnston is returned from Ireland he'll tell You, & carry it, for he has done so by many before
Thursday April 30, 1767
Dr George.

In the first place give my best Wishes, & Services to my Partner, & tell him, that I believe his Suspicions are well founded - He may be well-assur'd that I with not suggest ye Smallest hint of what I know to
Colman don't imagine, Mr George, that I am such a booby - Colman has told me that he has an affair to open to Me, but we have always been interrupted by Somebody, or another, so I have not yet had ye Whole, & which he has some qualms in bringing out - however I am prepared, & he will be surprised at my little concern & Ease upon this Occasion - I am sure there is Something in it, & yet ye more I think of it, ye more I am puzzled: Who finds Money? - What is the plan? Who are ye directors? damn me if I comprehend it, but I shall know more - suppose You & Mr Lacy meet me at his house at Isleworth next Wednesday Morning, I will come from Hampton, & be with You at his own time, & he may return to Town again - you may send me a Note by ye Hampton Stage Tuesday Next Which I shall receive at the time I arrive there, & pray send the two Reviews for Becket , or what other things You may have for Me. pray mind that - I think we should meet directly - I am glad Vernon has signed - & I think we shd close with Earn , but let Mr Lacy determine.

My Wife desires You to write a Note ye Night you receive this (Saturday) to our Maid at Hampton, Nancy Hetherington to prepare some Mutton , & a pudding with some Asparagus for our dinner on Tuesday about 5 o'Clock - rather Six . pray get me all ye News to send on Tuesday by ye Coach. What, has Holland no hand in this? - is he hummed? - I have not ye least Idea of ye Matter nor have I ye least Notion of them doing any thing to give Us one moment of uneasiness - I hope Mr Lacy thinks so too - God bless You & Yours my wife Sends her Love to You all.
D Garrick
PS. Remember ye Newspapers for Reading & a Slice of News - I shall let you know with C- Says. -
January 15th 1769
Dear Sir,

I would not willingly hinder your raising the devil for the Northampton Election; and, therefore, I have avoided breaking in upon you. - If you have dispatched the old gentleman (for Mr. Lane tells me you have been of late much locked up), I should be glad you would come abroad again, and see your earthly friends. - Pray let us settle our Zenobia accounts: we have many pounds of yours in our
hands - Have you settled with Davies? Will you have my note, or will you have more money - Speak and have, Master Ford!

When shall we talk about certain Dramas, or Drama? will you make me the guardian of your dramatic fame, or will you renounce, at once, the devil and all his works, except those which may call your honour to Westminster-hall, or to the Bar of the House of Commons. - I am almost afraid to speak, and yet I cannot be silent. - I would have been with you to-day, but I am going to take a little air at Hampton.
Madame Riccaboni sends you a volume and a note.
Ever and truly yours,
D. Garrick
July 30th 1770
Dear Madam.
You cannot imagine how much I think Myself honoured by Your most flattering, friendly letter - the Moment I received it, at my return from Hampshire this day, I sit down to answer it -

You may be assured, that no Care shall be wanting on my part to do Justice to ye Author of the Bon ton : I shall not read it in ye Common way, but think twice, before I speak my Mind - if I can see a Merit in it proper for ye Stage, You may depend upon it, that I will show my regard to You, by my Zeal in promoting Its Success: Should I think Otherwise, I should pay a very ill compliment to your friendship, & my own Sense of it, if I did not speak to You, as Your Shakespeare phrases it, as to my thoughts, as I do ruminate . Sorry, very Sorry am I to hear both for ye Sake of ye Author, Stage, & Manager, that a certain Lady has not had, even ye tip of her Finger in the Dramatic pie - if she had I would have underwritten it unseen, & unheard -

You have had such wondrous Success in Smuggling, I could wish that you would try another Venture, & take me into partnership - but what a parcel of stuff I am writing, & in the midst of much Company, without fear, or Wit! - I must tell you, that Mrs Garrick (Who begs her best respects may be presented to You) & I set out immediately for Lincolnshire thence to Cambridgeshire, & shall not return home these three Weeks or a Month - I will not pretend to read ye Play, till my return, & then it shall be ye first thing I will do - the Author should know that We are at this Moment Engaged to more plays, & petites pieces than we can act for the two Winters to come, unless any of the Authors of them should choose to withdraw in performances.

Pray, dear Madam, accept of this galloping &, I am afraid you'll say, Stumbling Epistle, as ye mere overflowings of a Warm heart, highly Sensible of Your friendship, & favour - You see, how I can trust Your feelings, while I am afraid of Your Understanding -
I am Mrs Montagu's most faithful & Obliged humble Servant
D: Garrick.

upon reading over my hasty letter, I find I have impertinently offered myself as a partner in Smuggling - that is - wishing You
would as secretly write a play, as you did a certain Essay, & that I, as Manager, might partake of ye plot & ye Profits. To Mrs Montagu at Denton near Newcastle upon Tyne.
Hampton Augst 22 1770
My Dear Madam
The Day after I returned to this Place, I did the thing the most agreeable to Me - obeyed Your Commands -

I read over the Comedy with a most uncommon prejudice in It's favour, & Sorry, very sorry I am to say, that with all the influence Mrs Montagu has, & Ever shall have upon Me, I could not turn, or twist my Mind to approve of the Performance: The Scenes are merely dialogues without the least interest in the fable, or indeed Enough of a Story to carry on ire Attention - I likewise think that the Characters are not Well marked, & that the vis comica is wanting through the Whole - Lady Ethrington bids the fairest for a dramatic personage; but she is not new - the follies of her Ladyship have been so highly & exquisitely exposed in one of the last Dialogues in Lord Littleton's Collection, that I should be afraid of It's Success upon the Stage. there is, notwithstanding all I have said, and I cannot conceal, nor will Ever Endeavour to cloak my opinion from You, there is a certain Merit in the Writing of the dialogue but wholly void of dramatic force & interest to give it Success in the representation - I shall return to London next Sunday Evening, when I will carefully convey the Comedy to your house in Hill Street - It gives me great Uneasiness to send You these, my Sincere Thoughts upon a Work, for the Author of Which You express so great a regard.
I flatter Myself that You will trust in my Sincerity, what Ever doubts (& I have many Myself) You may have of my Judgment.
I am most truly Ire Obliged & Obedt
D Garrick
Mrs Garrick presents her Respects, & I beg Mine to Mrs Montagu.
To Mrs Montagu at Denton near Newcastle upon Tyne.
Dear Brother.

I sit down at this time to do a most disagreeable thing to me, which is to tax you with Neglect, unkindness, & I will not add injustice to Me - I have Suffered much of late, I have hid my uneasiness as well as I could, I have had Moments of good Spirits, but my Mind has still returned to You, & your behaviour to Me - some late circumstances have brought this letter somewhat forwarder than I intended it, & a Weight upon my thoughts have pressed me to disclose 'Em to You - I shall not Accuse You of being always uneasy when You are with Me, & Your excuse of business to get away as soon as possible, I think that would be Weakness in Me, & ye only Way not to remedy it; but as I imagine such seeming unkindness proceeds from Your unwillingness to hear my complaints, Your visits of hurry are not unnatural - but to ye business - did I Ever keep any Concern of any kind from You, have I not always opened my heart, & designs to You, have You not had permission to open my letters, & know Every thing about me, & my affairs? - have you returned this kindness? - have you not been possessed sometime of a Country house of horses, Chariot &c without so much as in ye least hinting it to Me? - had you been possessed of ye fortune of Lord Clive such a Brother (as (I
think) I think I have been to You) should have been in common civility at least acquainted with it - I have never heard of it but from ire Neighbours, to whom I have always expressed my ignorance - an old Clergyman attacked me at Court on ye Birthday as Your Neighbor in ye Country - What is this Mystery? - if I was not kindly to be admitted into ye secret, surely I had a right to be a partaker of it - but let that be passed over - I can have my separate Secrets, if I please, & at least balance that Account with You - I have likewise no right, perhaps I have not, to ask how Your Circumstances can bear this load of Expense, & whether it is not strange with ire family, & complaints of hard times, hard relations &c that you have voluntarily taken a load upon You, which, I fear, you are not able to bear - if it is said, for that has been dropped, (for I hear more than I could wish) that Mr Carrington insisted upon ire having it, or taking it - this mends not ye matter with Me - I am still unkindly treated - I must tell You too, that You did not please me by sending ye Receipt to Mr Hoar to get money from my tenant G-f? how could you know in With manner I intended to act by him, & ire not telling me of it, till I had exposed Myself, was a most disagreeable Circumstance: I must for ye future Insist that no Monies of Mine, upon any Account are taken up without my Receipt from any one Person whatsoever - I come now to my request - which is that You make me acquainted with the State of Fermignac's Acct - You know that I had resolved not to pay a Shilling of ye Jubilee business but by ye Money owing to Me then - I now calmly assure You, that I will not: I had (I think generously) determined to pay the debts of ye adventurers of ye Jubilee - I told You I would pay 'Em with ye Legacy-Money - I told You to make a partition of it, & that I was ready to give any Security for paying my portion of any after debts, if they shd come in - if You had consulted the Spirit of ye deed, it shd not have been dragged on to this time, to make what would have been a piece of Generosity quickly done, a flat tame Action so laggingly performed - I must entreat You to lay ye account before Me, that I may Act accordingly - I can have no pleasure in knowing more of your Secrets, than what immediately concern Me, But these I have a right to, & my affairs demand that I be instructed immediately - You have known my Wishes, my uneasiness upon this Matter, & I wish You had done it before & openly from Yourself -
I am Dear Brother in expectation of ire Compliance with my request. Yrs Sincerely,
D Garrick
Friday Night
Dear George

To begin with my Wife's business first - she desires you to take notice that Mrs Hale & Mrs Calvert have her Box tomorrow Night -
She likewise prays you to send to Mrs Pot to offer her ye Box at some of ye benefits She shall choose: He has been particularly civil & she hopes you will not neglect to send Jim to 'Em in Lincoln's-Inn-fields - We have forgot ye George & Ribbon for ye Picture, my Wife thinks that she put it in a brown glove next drawer to yt where the Keys are, if not there, look into ye door of ye bookcase and under ye books & which is next to ye door as you come in to ye bed chamber - When ye little door is opened, there is a drawer, & she may have put ye George there - If Dance is not gone send that (well packed up) & ye Papers & letters by him, if not by ye Stage - Ire sheme of sealing up the Keys, we desire you will do, as it will be one trouble, Should Mr Wyld send for ye Map of Hendon, (& I am surprised he has not) it lies told up in Common paper upon ye Harpsicord - ye Map may be brought down, & left in ye forroom, but give ye damned maid great cautions about it. Tell Johnston I used but four Tickets for ye Messiah , ye other two are wrapped up in ye little table by ye Settee I generally sit upon. how did Miss Hayward come off? I forgot to speak about it - Pope had a Bargen If the Mayor of Garratt shd be done Foot will make a pretence to get up ye West-Indian - some Eye shd be upon yt - I could be glad to know, when I must write to Dick Burke : the Brothers can inform You, where you give, or send ye warrant. I forgot to speak to Johnston to let Miss Bathurst have a side box, (if one drops) for ye first or 2d time of ye West-Indian - Will not you insinuate that the West Indian will be performed on Thursday in Passion Week? I am very unhappy about Wyld, so connected with him, & he so idle - or (which I can't think) so careless of my Interest - I know not what to do - Clutterbuck has written twice, to rouse him - I speak, entreat & Every thing else, but he does not go on - It is strange he did not send for the map - Suppose you was to send a Card to know, if he wants it, for I had left such a charge about it, & have written to know if Mr Wyld has sent for it - the Bitch of a Maid may be knocking when he sends, & ye Copy-holders may be his foes, because he is my friend - It is hard to know, & yet I am distressed about him - he has all ye Papers & knows ye matters of ye manor so well - I can't help it, & so I'll go sleep, if my foot will let me, for it is very painful indeed. did You speak to Lord Pembroke about David's leave to follow his Military Studies at ye Academy - ?
I can no more so adieu till next time - Yrs most affecly

D: Garrick
I must entreat when you go to my house to do ye above business, that you will see my poor cat fed with ye milk we have sent for her - if you don't see her dip her whiskers in it, that unfeeling devil in ye house, will make up a Sack posit to dip Cautherly's chin in. Should you discover anything - pray put somebody into ye house & turn her out directly . Ask for ye milk, & say you promised Me to see her fed.
Hampton Sunday 15th 1771 My dear Madam.
We have been very unhappy at Your indisposition, much flattered with Your letters, but at ye same time glad that You have not risked your health to do Us honour, & give Us true pleasure:

I am not so Selfish to Wish to Enjoy your Mind without It's being well supported by Your natural Spirits - had I been one of Seneca's Friends, I should have desired to be excused attending ye opening Of his Veins, notwithstanding the wonders they relate of his preaching from ye Bath.

your alarm from Mr Montagu I hope will be much abated before You receive this - the fears, & anxieties for these Children; may they repay You in gratitude, tenderness & Affection - ! they are very fortunate, & must if they live (for I cannot suppose your Nephews to want either heads or hearts) be happy in themselves, & comforts to Mr Montagu & Yourself. We have had an Excellent day with ye Prince - he is reserved, but Easy - Says little, but to the purpose - an Old Friend of Mine, MonSr Grimm, a kind of German Frenchman, (no bad Mixture) attended him; he is lively, clever, & honourable - beloved by his friends, & has no Enemies - I told him of ye feast I had Endeavoured to procure for him, & he felt ye loss of it, as if he really knew You. a small Note of one Line & a half, left in Southampton Street Either to morrow, or ye next day will make Us happy, if it assures Us that you are well, & have no more apprehensions about ire Nephew - My Wife sends her most affect respects, & is made not a little proud by ye manner you have Spoken of her -
I am Madam most truly Your devoted
D: Garrick
I am so cramped with writing a hundred letters that I can scarce hold my pen to write legibly.
My dearest Madam.

I have indeed of late been balancing the Account of good & Evil, and as I have been a great debtor for the real pleasures of last
Summer, I have been called to a Severe payment by a fit of ye Stone - I am at present in Heaven, & resolute enough to fulfil a promise I made to ye Prince of Hesse Darnstadt to play ye part of Lusignan for him to Night, as he must leave London to Morrow - Mrs Garrick, (whose admiration of You exceeds that of Women, & not in ye least lessened by her knowing that You are the Goddess of my Idolatry) would have paid her respects, had not her very affectionate attendance & care of me for some weeks past, employed her Wholly - We shall go to Hampton toMorrow as ordered by ye faculty, & at our return we shall certainly, dead or alive, as an Irish Captain once said to Me, pay our respects in Hill Street.
Most unalterably Your faithful & devoted
David Garrick
I write, or rather scrawl from my Couch. To Mrs Montagu.
Hampton Wednesday night My Dear Sir,

I brought The Grecian Daughter with me here, have examined her well, and am wonderfully pleased with the Lady. Mrs. Garrick was more affected than ever I knew her to be with any play: - I will never take your word again in any of your own matters. - I have a few objections; chiefly, I think, in the third act - but they are of no consequence, or rather they may be easily got over, if you agree with me. - The part of the Daughter is one of the finest for an actress in all the dramatic circle. - If Barry will take pains with the Father, it will be of great service to him, though second to the Lady. - I wish you and myself joy - finish the fifth act as fast as you can; and pray let me see you either Friday morning at the house, or in the evening in Southampton-street. I would call upon you, but you know too well my present care and hurry to stand upon ceremony.
Yours ever and most truly,
D. Garrick.
Arthur Murphy, Esq. Lincoln's Inn.
Hampton May 2d 1772
My dear Madam

You had much better stupefy YourSelf with Adam & Eve here, & breathe the fresh air of May 14 Miles from London than racket about in the Smoky Atmosphere of London - I could wish that Your Supreme Spirit on ye full gallop would but just recollect, that It has a body (alas for us not ye Stoutest) to drag after it - You can never die, but You will hurry off Your flesh by degrees, upon Earth, & then Your Spirit having shaken off encumbrances will mount to It's proper Element & habitation, & repose itself to all Eternity. I shall miss You some fine Morning, & upon Enquiring after You, Some of my astronomical friends will tell Me, that You passed over Saint Pal's about a quarter after Eleven - to be serious, for I am amazed at myself that I can dare to write ye above nonsense to you, as true Christians rest one day in Seven, You who are better than they, ought to rest two - & as I know those days would be the most terrible to you of the whole Week, I could wish You to have a few failings, that You might by way of Penance be Obliged to pass Your black letter days at Hampton - if I run on tormenting You with this ribaldry, I shall not have room for business - Saturday Sen'night & Sunday I am Engaged - Don Felix demands me on ye first, & on ye Second I am Engaged to Lord Shelburne & my french friend - I am at this Moment a most miserable being, Lady Pennyman (whom I don't know, nor ever will) will not give up her side box, & unless you will take possession of your Suspended Handbasket over ye Pit for ye first time, what shall I do for You? - I will stir Heaven & Earth -
drink up Eisel, Eat a Crocodile,

rather than You shall not have ire will - but perhaps You'll think better of it, & avoid the Theatre this Warm Weather - vain as I am of ire presence when I Enact, I had much rather You would avoid a crowded, hot Steamy theatre, which defies All the Powers of Ventilators - rest rest perturbed Spirit ! that my fidgety Soul should be preaching & giving Advice to Wisdom herself is surely very ridiculous - it puts me in Mind of a Sensible Neighbor of Mine - who with ye gravest Countenance, begged & beseeched me, not to hurry or fret myself about any thing - I heard him, & was much
touched with his manner, & affectionate expressions of friendp & concern for Me - & pray Mr Rayner (said I) do You never fret, & hurry Yourself? - O damn it (Swore he) that I do from Morning to Night, & for that reason I am the best able to give you my advice - Mutato Nominee de Me .
I know what is best for ye same reason, and therefore can advise it, but I want wisdom for practice - I need say no more, but that I am
most devotedly Mrs Montagu's
D Garrick.
PS. I will stay here till Monday. My Wife presents her respects -
I have scribbled so fast I can't read it myself - I was born to torment you -
Adelphi Decr 6 - 1772
A thousand thanks, my dear Madam, for your very balsamic Letter. I am this moment arrived & can not Even take my Lixivium till I have shown my gratitude.

I am much better in my health since I went out of Town, & quite recovered in Mind since I rec'd Ire Wise, feeling, charming friendly ten-thousand-Epithet-Epistle - I must show it Madam that is pose: Mrs Vezey in Town & my heart have no additional flutter? -

I believe if my blood shd freeze in my heart this very cold weather, that it would liquefy, like St Januarius's at ye Sight of ire hand Writing - indeed my good Lady, You have made me quite Easy - I love Lord Lyttelton, & would not lose him for Millions - When I can know that our attendance will not be impertinent, We Shall be as punctual in Hill Street, as the first Lady there (or in any Street), is punctual in making her friends & Admirers happy.
Most devotedly Yours
D: Garrick.
I write with ye Gout in my fingers.
To Mrs Montagu, Hill Street.
Adelphi - Sepr 24. 1773
Dear Peter.

I must recommend, (not with ye usual form, & Spirit of recommendation), but with all my Power & influence, if it extends so far as the City of Lichfield, my old Friend & Acquaintance Mr George Alexander Stevens , a Name well known, & a Person deservedly applauded, for his Peculiarity of Genius, & Universal Love of Mirth & Letters - He has great Merit, & more than all he is a very honest, liberal-minded Man, & deserves Every Encouragement that has been given to him - As he is travelling Your Way with his heads, I must beg leave to introduce him to You, & ire friends, not my dear Peter, that I think You & Ire friends want the least Amendment of Ire Own, but that You may laugh with my Friend Stevens
at ye heads of other People - In short, I have so great a desire that he Should be well received, & approved at my own Native Place, (as I always call it, tho dropped at Hereford) that I beg You will let ye Whole Town know that I beg it, as a particular favour, that they will attend his Lectures - If any should be discontented with his Performance, I beg that I may treat them, & that You will pay for all the Malcontents, & draw upon Me for the Sum total - I need not desire You, to let him taste ire Lichfield Mutton & best Ale, Your Own Heart always prevents my Wishes in these Matters. always in a hurry -
Dear Peter
If the Ladies expect a Maccaroni Player in Master George, they will be dreadfully disappointed -
To Peter Garrick Esq, Lichfield.
Adelphi Friday
My Best And Most Amiable Friend -

When you called last Night my foot was flanell'd up with ye Gout, and a Sight of you, and ten words from You, would have been a Charm for ye foul Fiend - but I was ordered to see Nobody, & did not know it was my cure till it was gone - I am much better, & so well, that I shall be able to appear in Old Lusignan tonight, & in a better Character tomorrow in Hill Street - in that of the faithful Friend, & admirer of Mrs. Montagu - I was reading, or rather dozing over the cold, Northern Critic when you were at the door - notwithstanding his flattery to me, I can't bear the unfeelingness of his Soul. Shakespeare no Tragic Poet! - Shakespeare not the first Tragic poet! - What insensibility! - but more of this when I have ye honour of seeing you tomorrow, which I most certainly will do, tho I am carried in a Litter & so laid at ire feet.
Dear Madam, most unalterably & faithfully yrs,
D. Garrick.
I am always kissing Miss Gregory's hand & will make her cry if possible tonight.
Drury Lane Theatre Monday Decr 12 1774 My dear George.

I was much rejoiced at your letter, & I hope your friend Dr Faulkener will land You safe again amongst Us - I shall always hold him in great Esteem for his Care & attention, & am ready to give him more solid proofs of my Gratitude:

I have this moment finished ye long part of Hamlet, & my hand trembles while I am writing with ye worst Pen in ye world - Johnston is in a damned humour, & I dare not ask for a better - We go on well, & shall play the Choleric Man for the first time on Monday Next - I was resolved to have it perfect & to do Every thing in my Power for it - I am surprised that he did not write to me by this post, however I trust I shall have one tomorrow, & then I shall be Easy - Ire Sons are Well & Mr Carrington says when he is better he will come to see Me - What can he have to communicate?
The 2d Hospital has never sent for a Bill nor do I know where to go after them - so we shall have only one this Season -
Foot is arrived & in great Spirits - he asked much after You - they are now playing Dibdin's Nonsense & as it met with some disapprobation ye first night We wish it well over -
There is a good ballad or two, ye rest Washy & Slop Dawdry - I really cannot write any more - they make a great Noise in ye house
Yours Ever & truly
D Garrick.
I believe it will be damned -
The Cobbler has met with much Obstruction - To George Garrick esq, three Tuns, Bath.
Adelphi March 27 1775
Dear Madam -

A new Footman, who being deaf, is not moved with the concord of sweet Sounds, - & being unmercurial in his heels could not overtake the Coach, prevented us from having the pleasure we devoutly (being Sunday) wished for last night - I could have brained the fellow - a Son of Dr. Robertson was with us, & we talked of Nothing but Mrs. Montagu, & Miss Gregory - Mrs. Garrick was indeed just returned from Hampton & my Elder Brother was screwing up his Features to a parting ditty, which he sighed forth, & left us before 5 this morng. The fool was so deaf he could
not tell us where you ordered ire Coachman to drive, so that we could do nothing but fret and scold. I had two great favours to ask: the one was to beseech you not to be impressed by any Acct of a late Separation from the house of Cumberland, till you have heard the calm truth from ire humble Servant - Such ingratitude! but I won't say any more at present, but be assured I will never do anything to any one Creature, that shall make You (& that is my only concern) think less favourably of me.
Suspend your Justice till the Cause is heard : Your understanding naturally does this, & I flatter myself that your heart will not easily be misled to condemn me -

Something too much of this, - the next favour I had to solicit was Your name, which I more Glory in than if Possessed & to be added to ye most noble list I have got for a very ingenious man who has undertaken 6 etchings from the principal Characters of Shakespeare. I have sent you a Sample of the work, which I must beg you to return to day or tomorrow - without your permission I have placed you at the head of my List, & Everybody agrees to the propriety of having such a Leader - Should you meet with any choice Spirits, whose names may be easily got, they will not discredit themselves, & do great Service to a most ingenious Man. - I am Madam with every Sense of Esteem & affection most devotedly Yours,
D. Garrick.

Mrs. Garrick presents her respects - I would send more than these to Miss Gregory were I not afraid of Mrs. Garrick's Curiosity wishing to read over this letter. I have had a little pain & worse symptoms this morning.
Almacks Novr 7th 1775
Dear George.

We rejoice at your visible alteration of health & Spirits - Palmer says, that you begin to pick up, I don't mean at ye Whist Table, but in Your looks - pray keep yrself quiet in Mind & ire Body will get better of course - I beg you will let me know the progress of your health & I likewise must insist that you never think of leaving that fountain of Your health, till you can show us a pair of rosy Cheeks, Spirited eyes, and a Belly out of the perpendicular - the Little Gypsy goes on Hummingly, & rises nightly in repute - there was a little odd talk of some party against us, but to this Minute there has not been one Single disapprobation - Weston is dying, & with him goes a good Actor, & a very bad Man - Mrs King is useful, but not excellent - she stops gaps but will not allure - Ire Son David is not yet arrived, he is they say, at Lichfield with his Uncle - all the rest of ire Olive Branches are well, Mr Carrington is better & worse & will continue so, till he dyes - I shall write to you by Palmer - just let us know that you are better -
Ever & affecty Yrs
D Garrick
G. Garrick Esqr, Bath.
Adelphi March 21st 1776
Dear Peter

Your Ale is exquisite & I must reward the Brewer, & pay my debts honestly - I wish from my Soul that I could tell You when I shall be at Lichfield, but till I have given my Successors possession, & received my Money I can't stir from ye Property - the day of payment is the 24 of June, & till that happy day is past, I shall not think myself my own Master - but then, I shall shake off my Chains, & no Culprit at a Jail delivery will be happier - I really feel ye Joy, I used to do, when I was a boy at a breaking up: I receive Every honour that a Man can do from all Sorts of people, & I was yesterday enrolled a member among the first & greatest people in this Kingdom - We have a New house built in the best Taste in ye middle of St James's Street, & it is furnished like a palace - Each Member pays 12 Guineas at Entrance - It is ye first Society for titles & property in the known world - I need not tell You that with all this & 14 Dukes at the head of us, that I never was duller in all my Life. I made my best bows to my Brethren, graces and Royalty, drank a Glass of Lemonade to keep me awake, which grip'd Me, the Effects of which I found burdened me & went home as fast as I could. - Dr Johnson & Mr Boswell will be at Lichfield almost as soon as this - he is coming to take his leave of you all before his departure for Italy -

You are Johnson's prime favourite - I was sorry not to see Mr Fletcher, I sent after him, the Moment I got up, to his Hotel, but he was flown, & I could never after catch him - I am angry that Mr Lamb would not call upon me again - pray our Loves to all - My Wife will soon answer her Neice's letter - the Bell rings -
Yours most affecty

D: Garrick
George is again ailing I fear he never will be well. I am better, but not quite well - could I get rid of the pain at ye Neck of my bladder, which is lately much better, I should have no complaint -
Hampton April 12th 1776
Dear George.

As Mr Linley sets off for Bath on Sunday morning, I chose to write by him rather than the Post: it gave Us great Pleasure that Your Change of Places has made such a Change in Your health - I think that Bath for You, is what the Roman Catholics think of their religion, there is no Salvation out of it - You should be absolutely resolved to fix Your Standard there - Your Girls & David are almost well, very little remains of their Cough - I shall transplant them next Sunday to their new apartments which their Grandmother has prepared for them, a fine bed on the first floor, but David's bed is taken down in Nat's room - what meanness! - they have forced the Lad to sell out, which has backened him some Years in Life, & now they turn him out to starve, if some Chapter of Accidents is not turned over in his favour - last Night I played Drugger for ye last time - the Morning Post will tell You ye whole of that Night - I thought ye Audience were Mad, & they almost turned my brain:

I must desire that my good friend Mr Squire, to whom I beg my best Wishes, & You would consider what our friend Linley means to give Me as a Security, for part of his Share: he is to raise £10 000 & wishes me to take some houses &c he has in Bath, which you will see, besides his Share, as a Security for the Mortgage - he likewise wants me to take 4 & 1/2 Pcent - I demur to that, for as I have 5 from Lacy, will it not appear wrong to take less from a new purchaser, & for a less Sum? - pray both think of that & talk ye whole matter over together, & with Linley, & let me know, what it is, that I may do. He is a very honest man, but I must be secure, or what have I been doing? Love to all friends -
Yours Ever & Affecly
D Garrick.
My Wife sends her Love.
Augst the 19th 1776
Dear Peter.

We have at last settled our peregrinations - they stand thus - the Duke of Devonshire meeting me 3 Weeks ago at Lord Sponsor's at Wimbleton, desired me, in so affectionate Manner to go to Chatsworth that I could not resist him - Lady Spencer, the first of Women, hearing what was passing, insisted, as affecty that we should be there at ye Same time with them - which will be in ye first Week of ye next Month September - We have therefore resolved to go ye Second or Third to Chatsworth & after being there four or five days at Most, we will be with You at Lichfield for some days - George's Children are with their Grandfather, who is very ill, & does not care to part with them; so we shall come alone to You, & if You will let us keep house for a Week, with Some assistance to Mrs Betty, we will drink soft ale, & laugh like ten Christ'nings - we had rather live simply, Mutton & Pudding than upon all the
dainties in the world - Ben Victor who is at Mr Piggot's will meet Us at Lichfield, & I shall take him up to Town with Us - I wish among You, that you could get him a bed -
I will give both him & You notice when I shall beat up ire Quarters - We intend this time, to be like Bobadil, not too popular, or generally visited - private is ye word -
If you like our Scheme say the Word, and we will be punctual - Our Loves to all of You.
Ever & Affecly Yours
D: Garrick
Send ye enclosed as soon as You conveniently can -
Octr 26 1776
Dear Madam.
I congratulate all Your friends & Myself among that honourable, happy Number for Your safe return to us -

Mrs Garrick did herself the honour of calling upon You to return her thanks in Person for the great care you have taken, & the trouble you have had, with the friendly favour of Mrs Necker to her - I heard with pleasure of ire being at the french Academy when Voltaire exhibited his malevolent Nonsense (for which too among other Obligations I thank You) upon our beloved & immortal Shakespeare: could any thing possibly add to my Admiration of Mrs Montagu, it was the Expression of contempt & astonishmt which, I hear You put on, at hearing the Weak and impotent ravings of Age, Envy, hatred & Malice - it rejoices Me much to hear, that this unchristian attack upon Genius had not a favourable reception even from his own friends -

I doubt not, but You have converted Numbers to the faith, not with Sword as Mahomet did, but by those emanations of Genius, which You have caught from the divinity You have so powerfully, & justly protected & admired - this Attack of Voltaire, I hope, is not to pass unnoticed - If the Champions will not mount with the regulars, the Light horse, & hussars must begin a Skirmish - I most devoutly wish for the honour of a little conversation, which I should immediately have Endeavoured to enjoy in Hill Street, had not a Small attack of ye Gout obliged me to Stay at home for a day or two. Yet may I not hope for that favour, as soon as the more important Matters have had their first dues, & we with our little demands may present ourselves with all Love, & humility?
I am Dr Madm Ire most devoted Served
D. Garrick
Mrs Garrick presents her respects - I with Send my best Wishes, with my Wife's, to Miss Gregory, but alas, I fear the enchantments of french Everything has destroyed all my hopes -
I with not have sent this Scrawl could I have written better, but ye illbred Gout has prevented me
April ye 18 1777?
My good Madam.

I only requested the gentle Stream of Your Bounty, & you have flowed upon Us with a torrent - I am really ashamed of being ye means of Your abundant kindness to Us - I have a Set of friends, whom I intended to call upon Every year for one pound one - as I cannot return the Overplus, I have set it down in my Book over against Your never to be forgotten Name - par advance 5 Years - 5:5:0 give me leave to let you into a little Secret history of this Charity - a Nobleman in your Street whom I visit & who looks like benevolence itself - had a Ticket from Me at ye same time, that I was impertinent enough to send one to You - Your two Names like A fat & lean rabbit in a poulterer's Shop - stand thus together -
Mrs Montagu 5:5:0 - no ticket
Rt. Honble Lord: W. de Be 0:5:0 - one ticket.
Mrs Garrick presents her Respects, with Mine & I at the feet of Miss Gregory am
My dear Madam Most devotedly yrs
D Garrick

before I went out of Town I sent to Holy, but could not find him then, since my return I have been confined with a Sore throat & hoarseness, & cannot yet Stir out - if You have any orders of any kind for your faithful Servant, you may depend upon my Executing them with care & fidelity.
Mrs Montagu, Hill Street.
Wynnstay Denbeighshire Sepr 26 1777 Dear Peter

We shall certainly be at Birmingham on Sunday Evening the 5th of October , & shall stay ye Next day till about 12, so we may have a good deal of Gabble; I hope You will bring Cousin Bailey with You, & let us have a Snug party - I send this by the Chester post,
& you may Send me an answer by ye Same Way - directed to me at Sr Watkin Williams Wynn's Baronet at Wynnstay near Wrexham, Denbeighshire to tell me if you approve ye Party, & it will be convenient - we are very happy here, & cannot stir till Saturday Sen'night the 4th of October - these Welch scenes are quite New to us, & very well worth anybody's Curiosity - at Shrewsbury the Town was in an Alarm at my Coming, & the Raven-Inn besieged - I little Expected so much honour from Salopian Swains, & Welch Mountaineers - their Observations upon my Person, age &c you shall have at Birmingham on Sunday ye 5th Octr if Nothing prevents your making Us happy - a line by ye return of the Post to Chester will oblige
Your most affect Brother
D: Garrick

The Ladies with Me Send their Love - Fosbroke desires her duty & Love to her Father & Mother - She hopes to see her Brother at Birmingham, who she tells me is gone there to be a Doctor - prays is it a Horse-Doctor?
Peter Garrick Esqr, Lichfield, Staffordshire.
Wynnstay Sepr 30th 1777
My dear Peter

Would it not be a little too much upon St Patrick, to desire You, Honey, to meet me at Birmingham & then return to Lichfield with You, which is much nearer my Dear - In short we beg to see You
at Birmingham next Sunday because we cannot Stay at Lichfield so long as we could Wish - Should You arrive Sooner than We - I beg You'll bespeak beds sufficient for Us all There will be two wanted for You & Cousin Dick - one for me & my Wife & one for Fosbroke & My Wife's Niece - I have Six horses for which I must have a good Stable & four Men Servants - Sr Watkin tells me it is a good house - We shall be there before Six in ye Evening -

I wish You would Order a good joint of Meat for ye Servants some fish if any, & some Chickens or fowls boiled or roasted as You like best & whatever Else you & Cousin choose to be ready about Seven or Sooner -
I am writing in ye Dark & Mr Parry ye famous Harper is playing like an Angel
Althorp Decr 15th 1777
Dear George

I have enclosed Lord Sandwich's Letter & my answer about Johnston , have I spelt his Name right? - if I have not You must
rectify it, & send Johnston with a Note to his Lordship with Your Respects, & direction Where He is to be found - I must desire You at ye Same time to speak to him about Moody, if my Security is not delivered up, I will never speak to him again.

If he gets once into a Sloop, we can upon his good behaviour, remove him with my Interest with my Lord - I have another thing to say - Miss More promised Me a Copy of the play to read to Lady Spencer if she has it ready & will send it on Friday Next to the Earl of Jersey, directed to Me , his Lordship will bring it down here on Saturday - if you have any Letters You may send them enclosed in ye Same parcel - You need not send me any more papers unless it is the Morning Chronicle, which Becket will take care of, Lord Spencer has all ye Papers Except that, I shd be glad to know what he says of ye Roman Sacrifice , Mr Cumberland has written an excellent Epilogue for it & that Be Master Yates would not speak it - Mr Cumberland will frank any thing for Me, & may be always found at Lord George Germaine's Office from ten to two - I believe ye office is Somewhere near Mr Rigby's - Will you speak to Captn Smith about Ironmonger in Lord Camden's & my Name - it with be done directly - I don't think Shirley will appear so Soon as Thursday - I hope not as it will be against his 6th Night -

I have sent a Letter for Jolliff ye Guardian to David's Girl - will it do? - if it will let it be directed & sent. I have promised Wilkes in Dublin a very Early printed Copy of Percy for his friend Ryder - pray take care to speak to Miss More for one as soon as it can be got, & Mr Chamier or Mr Cumberland will frank it to Mr Wilkes Sycamore Alley Dublin -
I am Yours Ever &c
D Garrick
remember to seal Lord Sandwich's letter after you have read it to Johnston - I hope the School for Scandal will be done on Friday, for Mr Mason - if ye New play perhaps he with choose That -

Let ye Play sent to Lord Jersey be made into as Slender a Roll as possible for he comes on horseback - his Lordship desires it - don't send anything Else with it - it must be at his house in Grosvenor Square on Friday Night at farthest -

Let' ye Play be cut as it is Acted - if it was printed off it with be better to read & I would stay a day or two for it. then You need not send to Lord Jersey's. Mr Chamier would frank it or Mr Cumberland -
George Garrick Esqr at the Stage Door of Drury Lane Theatre, Russel Street, Drury Lane (with Care & Speed).
